blocks.text:
Structured Query Language (SQL) is the standard language for defining, populating, querying and controlling relational data. A Java service rarely sends anything else to its database: every `PreparedStatement`, every Spring Data derived query and every Hibernate-generated statement is SQL by the time it reaches the server. A developer who reads SQL fluently can predict what an ORM sends, can diagnose why a statement is slow or wrong, and can replace generated code with a hand-written statement when the generated code is inadequate.

SQL is declarative. A statement describes the result that is required, not the steps used to produce it. The database planner chooses the access paths, the join order and the join algorithms (the subject of the query-processing chapters). Two consequences follow. First, equivalent statements can run in very different times, so the structure of a statement matters. Second, the order in which clauses are written is not the order in which they are evaluated, which is the most common source of confusion for new users and is treated in detail below.

This chapter and the following ones use one sample schema throughout: `departments`, `employees`, `customers`, `products`, `orders` and `order_items`. All outputs are real results from PostgreSQL 16.15 running on the build machine. Statements that differ in MySQL 8.x are shown beside the PostgreSQL form; MySQL output was not produced on the build machine and is labelled accordingly.

### The sample schema

The schema is small enough to be read in full and rich enough to expose every behaviour discussed in this part: a self-referencing foreign key (`employees.manager_id`), a nullable foreign key (`employees.dept_id`), a department without employees, customers without orders and a one-to-many-to-many chain from customers to orders to order lines.

blocks.text: *loaded in the examples; the self-reference on* `employees` *models the management hierarchy.*

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE departments (
  dept_id    integer PRIMARY KEY,
  dept_name  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  location   text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
  emp_id     integer PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name text NOT NULL,
  last_name  text NOT NULL,
  dept_id    integer CONSTRAINT emp_dept_fk REFERENCES departments(dept_id),
  manager_id integer CONSTRAINT emp_mgr_fk REFERENCES employees(emp_id),
  salary     numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (salary > 0),
  hire_date  date NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    integer PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  order_ts    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED'))
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   integer REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  line_no    integer,
  product_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
  qty        integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
);

blocks.text:
### Concept and mechanism

#### Statement categories

SQL statements are conventionally grouped by purpose. The grouping matters in practice because it determines privileges (a role may be allowed to read but not to change data), transactional behaviour (PostgreSQL executes DDL inside transactions, MySQL does not) and which tool a Java application uses to issue the statement.

rows: Group statements into units of work
blocks.caption: Statement categories.

blocks.text:
In PostgreSQL every statement, including DDL, is transactional: `BEGIN; DROP TABLE t; ROLLBACK;` leaves `t` intact. In MySQL (InnoDB) DDL statements cause an implicit commit and cannot be rolled back; a failed multi-step migration therefore leaves partial changes. This difference is significant for the migration chapter later in the book.

#### Logical processing order of SELECT

A SELECT statement is written in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, but it is evaluated logically in a different order: FROM (and joins) first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, the SELECT list, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and finally LIMIT/OFFSET. The planner is free to execute the physical steps in any order that yields the same result, so this is a rule about meaning, not about performance. The meaning explains which names are visible where.

blocks.text:
`annual` *exists only after the SELECT step, so WHERE and HAVING cannot reference it, while ORDER BY can.*

The following statement exercises every stage. On the sample data FROM yields 14 rows; WHERE removes employee 13 (no department, so the predicate `dept_id IS NOT NULL` is false) and the three employees with salary below 100000, leaving 10 rows; GROUP BY forms four groups; HAVING keeps the two groups with at least two members.

blocks.code:
SELECT dept_id, count(*) AS headcount, round(avg(salary)) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL AND salary >= 100000
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING count(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
LIMIT 3;

blocks.text: The statement filters rows first (WHERE), groups the survivors, discards groups with fewer than two members (HAVING), sorts the groups and returns at most three of them (two exist). The alias `avg_salary` is usable in ORDER BY because ORDER BY runs after the SELECT list. Using an alias in WHERE fails:

blocks.code: SELECT salary * 12 AS annual FROM employees WHERE annual > 2000000;

ERROR:  column "annual" does not exist
LINE 1: SELECT salary * 12 AS annual FROM employees WHERE annual > 2...
                                                          ^
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
PostgreSQL reports that the column does not exist. MySQL differs here: it also rejects an alias in WHERE but accepts an alias in GROUP BY and HAVING, an extension that PostgreSQL permits only in GROUP BY and ORDER BY (not HAVING). Portable SQL repeats the expression or wraps the query in a subquery or common table expression.

### Reading data: SELECT

#### Projection, expressions and aliases

The SELECT list may contain columns, constants, arithmetic, function calls and subqueries. `AS` introduces an alias; the keyword is optional but recommended because a missing comma between two column names silently turns the second into an alias of the first.

blocks.code:
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name,
       salary,
       salary * 12 AS annual,
       salary / 3 AS int_or_numeric
FROM employees WHERE emp_id IN (3, 10);

blocks.text:
String concatenation uses `||` in standard SQL and PostgreSQL. In MySQL `||` is by default a logical OR; the portable function is `CONCAT(a, b)`, which PostgreSQL also provides. Division of two integers truncates in PostgreSQL (`7 / 2` is 3), while the MySQL `/` operator always returns a decimal (`7 / 2` is 3.5000) and `DIV` performs integer division. The query above divides a `numeric` value, so the fraction is kept.

#### Filtering with WHERE

WHERE accepts a boolean expression. A row is kept only when the expression is TRUE; both FALSE and NULL (unknown) discard the row. This three-valued behaviour is detailed in the NULL chapter later in this part; the practical consequence is that `col = NULL` never matches and `IS NULL` must be used.

rows: `Pattern match: '%' any string, '_' one` `character; ILIKE is case-insensitive` `(PostgreSQL only)`

FROM employees
WHERE hire_date BETWEEN '2018-01-01' AND '2019-12-31'

blocks.text:
#### DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON

`SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate result rows, comparing all selected columns together and treating NULLs as equal to each other for this purpose. It is frequently used to hide a join that produced duplicates, which treats a symptom and not the cause (see the join chapter). PostgreSQL additionally offers `DISTINCT ON (expr)`, which keeps the first row of each group of rows that share the expression, where "first" is defined by ORDER BY. It has no MySQL equivalent; a window function is used instead.

---------+------------+-----------

The second statement returns the highest-paid employee of each department. The ORDER BY must begin with the DISTINCT ON expression; otherwise PostgreSQL rejects the statement.

#### ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET and FETCH

Without ORDER BY the order of result rows is undefined: the engine returns rows in whatever order its chosen plan produces them, and that order can change after an UPDATE, a VACUUM, a new index or a version upgrade. Any statement that uses LIMIT, a cursor or pagination must have an ORDER BY that is a total order, that is, one that never leaves two rows tied.

PostgreSQL and MySQL both accept `LIMIT n OFFSET m`. The standard form is `OFFSET m ROWS FETCH FIRST n ROWS` `ONLY`, supported by PostgreSQL (since 8.4), Oracle and SQL Server but not by MySQL. MySQL additionally accepts `LIMIT` `m, n` with the arguments in the opposite order, a frequent source of mistakes.

`WITH TIES` (PostgreSQL 13 and later) returns additional rows that tie with the last row on the ORDER BY key; the fifth row has salary 150000 and the sixth row ties with it, so six rows are returned by the second statement although five were requested. MySQL has no equivalent and uses a window function (RANK) instead.

NULLs sort after all non-null values in ascending order in PostgreSQL (and first in MySQL). `NULLS FIRST` and `NULLS LAST` control this in PostgreSQL; MySQL requires `ORDER BY col IS NULL, col`.

blocks.code: SELECT emp_id, dept_id FROM employees ORDER BY dept_id DESC NULLS LAST, emp_id LIMIT 4;

blocks.text:
### Changing data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, UPSERT

#### INSERT

`INSERT` adds rows. Listing the target columns is mandatory in application code: a statement without a column list depends on the physical column order and breaks when a column is added. Multiple rows can be inserted with one statement; a batch of N single-row statements costs N network round trips, while one multi-row statement costs one.

blocks.code:
INSERT 0 2
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "departments_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (dept_id)=(10) already exists.
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
The second statement violates the primary key. PostgreSQL aborts the statement and, inside a transaction, marks the whole transaction as failed (hence the `rb` wrapper used when producing this output). MySQL reports error 1062 "Duplicate entry '10' for key 'departments.PRIMARY'".

#### UPDATE and DELETE

`UPDATE` and `DELETE` without a WHERE clause affect every row. This is legal, silent and the cause of a well-known class of production incidents; the PITR section of the backup chapter later in the book recovers from one. Habit and tooling help: run the statement as a SELECT first, wrap it in a transaction and check the reported row count before committing. In MySQL the client option `--safe-updates` rejects UPDATE and DELETE without a key in WHERE.

blocks.code:
emp_id | first_name |  salary
--------+------------+----------
     10 | Rahul      | 88000.00
(1 row)

UPDATE 1
DELETE 1
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
PostgreSQL also supports `UPDATE ... FROM` and `DELETE ... USING` to modify rows by joining another table, which standard SQL expresses with subqueries; MySQL writes `UPDATE t JOIN u ON ... SET ...`.

#### RETURNING

`RETURNING` (PostgreSQL, also MariaDB 10.5 and later for some statements, but not MySQL 8.x) returns columns of the affected rows from INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in the same round trip. It is the reliable way to obtain generated keys and defaults and the basis of the "claim a row" queue pattern. In JDBC the portable route is `Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS`; the PostgreSQL driver implements it by appending `RETURNING` to the statement.

blocks.text:
#### UPSERT: ON CONFLICT and ON DUPLICATE KEY

An upsert inserts a row, or updates the existing row when a uniqueness constraint would be violated, as one atomic statement. The alternative written in application code (SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE) has a race: two sessions can both find the row missing and both attempt the insert. PostgreSQL uses `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (columns) DO` `UPDATE | DO NOTHING`; MySQL uses `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`. The conflict target in PostgreSQL names the unique index that acts as the arbiter; the pseudo-table `EXCLUDED` holds the row that was proposed.

blocks.text:
The MySQL `AS new` row alias requires 8.0.19 or later; older code uses the deprecated `VALUES(location)` function. When a table has several unique keys, MySQL fires the clause on whichever key conflicts first, which can update an unexpected row. PostgreSQL requires the conflict target to be named explicitly, which removes the ambiguity.

#### TRUNCATE

`TRUNCATE TABLE t` removes all rows by discarding the table files, which is far faster than `DELETE FROM t` for large tables and reclaims disk space immediately. It acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock in PostgreSQL, does not fire row-level triggers, and cannot be used on a table referenced by a foreign key unless the referencing tables are truncated in the same statement (`TRUNCATE a, b` or `CASCADE`). In PostgreSQL TRUNCATE is transactional and MVCC-safe; in MySQL it is DDL, commits implicitly and resets `AUTO_INCREMENT`. PostgreSQL resets sequences only with `RESTART IDENTITY`.

### Worked example: tracing one query by hand

The statement below lists, per department, the number of employees hired since 2019 whose salary exceeds 100000, ordered by that number. Evaluating it in logical order on the sample data gives the following trace.

The statement and its result are printed after the trace.

1. FROM and JOIN: 13 of the 14 employees match a department (employee 13 has a NULL `dept_id` and is discarded by the inner join); 13 joined rows exist.
2. WHERE: keeps employees hired on or after 2019-01-01 with salary above 100000. These are employees 4 (150000, 2019), 5 (120000, 2021), 7 (110000, 2020) and 14 (110000, 2024).
3. GROUP BY `dept_name`: Engineering receives employees 4 and 5, Sales receives 7 and 14. Two groups exist.
4. SELECT: `count(*)` is evaluated per group: 2 and 2.
5. ORDER BY: both groups have `n = 2`, so the tie is broken by `dept_name`.
6. The result is therefore (Engineering, 2) followed by (Sales, 2).

blocks.code:
SELECT d.dept_name, count(*) AS n
FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.hire_date >= '2019-01-01' AND e.salary > 100000
GROUP BY d.dept_name
ORDER BY n DESC, d.dept_name;

dept_name  | n
-------------+---
 Engineering | 2
 Sales       | 2
(2 rows)

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: pagination returns duplicate rows and skips others

**Scenario.** A support dashboard lists tickets sorted by priority, twenty per page, using `ORDER BY priority LIMIT 20` `OFFSET :page * 20`. Users report that some tickets appear on two pages and others never appear at all. The table `tickets` has 20,000 rows and only five distinct priority values.

**Symptoms.** The same `ticket_id` is visible on consecutive pages; a ticket known to exist cannot be found by paging; the effect is not reproducible after a restart and differs between environments. Page size 5 is used below for readability.

**Diagnosis.** The first step is to compare consecutive pages directly.

blocks.code:
SELECT ticket_id, priority FROM tickets ORDER BY priority LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;
SELECT ticket_id, priority FROM tickets ORDER BY priority LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

blocks.text: Ticket 20 appears at the top of both pages, and tickets 15, 25 and 10 are split inconsistently. All ten rows have priority 1, so ORDER BY gives no ordering among them. The second step is to confirm that the plan, not the data, differs between executions.

blocks.code:
QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=5 loops=1)
   ->  Sort (actual rows=5 loops=1)
         Sort Key: priority
         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 25kB
         ->  Seq Scan on tickets (actual rows=20000 loops=1)
(5 rows)

                         QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit (actual rows=5 loops=1)
   ->  Sort (actual rows=15 loops=1)
         Sort Key: priority
         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 25kB
         ->  Seq Scan on tickets (actual rows=20000 loops=1)
(5 rows)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
Both plans use a top-N heapsort, but the heap holds `OFFSET + LIMIT` rows (5 versus 15, visible as the row count of the Sort node), and a heap does not keep tied rows in a stable order. A different `OFFSET` therefore evaluates a differently sized heap and the tie order changes.

**Root cause.** `ORDER BY priority` is not a total order. SQL guarantees nothing about the relative order of rows that compare equal, so each execution may pick a different arrangement.

**Fix.** Add a unique tie-breaker, typically the primary key, so that the order is total. Then verify that consecutive pages are disjoint.

blocks.code:
SELECT ticket_id, priority FROM tickets ORDER BY priority, ticket_id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;
SELECT ticket_id, priority FROM tickets ORDER BY priority, ticket_id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

blocks.text:
The permanent fix has two parts. In the repository layer, every pageable query gets a unique final sort key. In Spring Data this means `PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("priority").and(Sort.by("id")))`; a `Pageable` that sorts by a non-unique property alone reproduces the defect. For deep pages OFFSET itself becomes the problem, because the server still produces and discards all skipped rows; keyset pagination (`WHERE (priority, ticket_id) > (:p, :id)` `ORDER BY priority, ticket_id LIMIT 20`) avoids this and is developed in the query-optimisation chapters.

**Prevention.** A code review rule: any `LIMIT` must be accompanied by an `ORDER BY` whose last element is unique. A test that pages through a table containing duplicate sort values and asserts that the union of the pages equals the table detects the defect.

#### Incident: UPDATE without WHERE (summary)

**Scenario.** A one-line salary correction is run without its WHERE clause in an interactive session with autocommit on. **Immediate action.** Stop writes if possible; autocommit means the change is already durable. **Fix.** Restore from a backup or by point-in-time recovery to a moment before the statement (see the backup chapter), or, when the previous values are known from an audit table, rewrite them from it. **Prevention.** Perform manual changes inside `BEGIN`, inspect the row count reported by the command (`UPDATE 14` when 3 were expected is the alarm), and only then `COMMIT`; give humans a role without direct write access to production tables.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot reference aggregates; HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can. A condition that does not involve an aggregate belongs in WHERE, because it reduces the rows before the aggregation work is done.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: In what order is a SELECT statement evaluated? FROM and joins, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT list (including window functions), DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT/OFFSET. This is the logical order that defines visibility of names; the physical execution order is chosen by the planner. It explains why an alias defined in SELECT can be used in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why can two executions of the same query return rows in different orders? Without ORDER BY the order is unspecified, and with an ORDER BY on non-unique columns the order among ties is unspecified. Plans, parallelism, vacuum activity and caching change it. Pagination therefore requires a total order, normally the sort key followed by the primary key.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP? DELETE removes selected rows, fires row triggers, writes one WAL record per row and can be filtered. TRUNCATE removes all rows by discarding storage, takes an exclusive lock and is much faster. DROP removes the table definition as well. In PostgreSQL all three are transactional; in MySQL TRUNCATE and DROP are DDL and commit implicitly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How is an upsert written in PostgreSQL and in MySQL, and why is it preferable to SELECT-then-INSERT? PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET ...; MySQL: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE .... The single statement is atomic and relies on the unique index, whereas SELECT followed by INSERT lets two sessions both observe the row as missing and one of them then fails or creates a duplicate.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What does RETURNING do and what is the JDBC equivalent where it is unavailable? RETURNING (PostgreSQL) returns columns of rows written by INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in the same round trip. Where it is not supported, as in MySQL 8, the application uses `Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` for generated keys, or a follow-up SELECT inside the same transaction.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is OFFSET pagination slow for deep pages, and what is the alternative? The server must produce and discard all skipped rows, so the cost grows with the offset. Keyset (seek) pagination filters with `WHERE (sort_key, id) >` `(last_key, last_id)` and uses an index, so the cost is independent of the page number.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
SQL fundamentals

- SQL is declarative; a statement describes a result, and the planner chooses the execution steps.
- The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT; it determines which names are visible in each clause.
- Result order is guaranteed only by an ORDER BY that is a total order; pagination without one duplicates and skips rows.
- UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE are legal; run them in a transaction and check the reported row count.
- Upserts (`ON CONFLICT`, `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`) and `RETURNING` replace racy read-then-write code and extra round trips.
- PostgreSQL DDL is transactional; MySQL DDL commits implicitly.

Relational design stores each fact once: a department name lives in `departments`, not in every employee row. A query that needs both facts must recombine the tables, and the JOIN operation does this. Most SQL defects found in production code are join defects: a missing row because an outer join was silently turned into an inner join, an inflated total because a join multiplied rows, or a slow report because the join condition could not use an index. This chapter defines each join type by the rows it produces, demonstrates the behaviour on the sample data and then treats the pitfalls.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Definition: a filtered Cartesian product

Conceptually every join starts from the Cartesian product of its two inputs (every row of the left table paired with every row of the right table) and keeps the pairs for which the join condition is true. The `ON` clause holds that condition. The join types differ only in what happens to the rows that have no partner.

rows: Inner result plus unmatched left rows
Left rows kept, right columns NULL
Inner result plus unmatched right rows
Right rows kept, left columns NULL
Inner result plus unmatched rows of both sides
Both kept, other side NULL (not in MySQL)
blocks.caption: Join types.

blocks.text: The inner join returns four rows; employee 13 disappears. The left join returns all five, with NULL in the department columns for employee 13. A RIGHT JOIN is a LEFT JOIN with the tables exchanged and is rarely written; reading queries is easier when one convention (left joins only) is used throughout a code base.

FROM employees e
FULL JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id

blocks.text:
The full join exposes both kinds of orphan: employee 13 without a department and department 50 without an employee. MySQL has no FULL JOIN; the equivalent is `LEFT JOIN ... UNION ... RIGHT JOIN ...`, or a `UNION ALL` of a left join and an anti-join.

#### USING, NATURAL JOIN and CROSS JOIN

`USING (col)` is shorthand for an equality on identically named columns and outputs the column once. `NATURAL JOIN` joins on every column name the two tables share; it silently changes meaning when a column is added or renamed, and should not appear in production code. `CROSS JOIN` has legitimate uses: generating combinations (a calendar of dates times a list of stores) and expanding data. An unintended cross join (a missing ON clause, or a missing predicate between three tables) multiplies row counts and is a typical cause of a query that never returns.

blocks.code:
SELECT count(*) AS cross_rows FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments;
SELECT count(*) AS accidental FROM employees e, departments d;   -- comma join with no WHERE

cross_rows

(1 row)

#### Self-join

A self-join joins a table to itself under two aliases and is the standard way to follow a one-level relationship such as employee to manager. The manager is optional, so a left join keeps the root employee.

blocks.code:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.emp_id <= 6
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

emp_id | employee | manager
--------+----------+---------

      2 | Vikram   | Asha
      3 | Meera    | Vikram
      4 | Ravi     | Vikram
      5 | Sneha    | Meera
      6 | Arjun    | Asha
(6 rows)

blocks.text:
Hierarchies of unknown depth need a recursive common table expression, treated in the subqueries chapter.

#### Semi-join and anti-join

A semi-join returns the rows of one table that have at least one match in another, without duplicating them and without exposing the other table's columns. An anti-join returns the rows that have no match. SQL has no dedicated keyword; both are written with `EXISTS`, `NOT EXISTS`, `IN` or a left join. The planner recognises these patterns and executes them with dedicated join strategies (Hash Semi Join, Hash Anti Join, Nested Loop Anti Join).

blocks.code:
-- semi-join: customers that have placed at least one order
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY 1;

-- anti-join: customers that have never ordered
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY 1;

-- equivalent anti-join with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY 1;

The IS NULL test in the last statement must reference a column that is never NULL in the right table (the primary key); testing a nullable column would also match real rows whose value is NULL. `NOT IN` is a third spelling that is dangerous when the subquery can return NULL; this is the subject of an incident in the subqueries chapter.

### Join algorithms in one page

The logical join type does not fix how the server computes it. PostgreSQL chooses between three physical algorithms for each join, based on estimated row counts and available indexes; the query-processing chapters later in this part show them in EXPLAIN output.

rows: For each outer row, probe the inner side (usually through an index)
Few outer rows and an index on the inner join column
Build an in-memory hash table on the smaller input, stream the larger input through it
Large unsorted inputs, equality conditions only
Sort both inputs on the join key (or read them from indexes) and merge
Inputs already sorted; large inputs; range-free equality
blocks.caption: Physical join algorithms.

blocks.text:
MySQL 8.0.18 introduced the hash join for equi-joins without usable indexes; before that, MySQL had only nested-loop variants (including block nested loop). Since MySQL has no merge join, a join of two large unindexed tables was historically much slower there than in PostgreSQL.

### Worked example: LEFT JOIN with aggregation, step by step

Requirement: for every customer, the number of orders and the total quantity ordered; customers without orders must appear with zeros. The statement joins three tables and aggregates.

The statement and its result are printed after the trace.

1. `customers LEFT JOIN orders`: customer 1 yields three rows (orders 101, 102, 106), customer 2 yields three (103, 104, 109), customer 3 two (105, 110), customer 5 two (107, 108), and customers 4 and 6 one row each with NULL order columns: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 12 rows.
2. `LEFT JOIN order_items`: every order row is expanded by its line count (order 101 has 2 lines, 102 has 1, and so on). Rows with a NULL `order_id` find no match and remain, with NULL item columns.
3. GROUP BY collapses the expanded rows per customer. Because step 2 repeats each order once per line, `count(*)` would overstate the orders; `count(DISTINCT o.order_id)` removes the repetition, and for customers 4 and 6 it ignores the NULL.
4. `sum(oi.qty)` is NULL for customers without orders; `coalesce` substitutes 0.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       count(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
       coalesce(sum(oi.qty), 0)   AS units
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-------------+-----------------+--------+-------

           2 | Bharat Stores   |      3 |    10
           3 | Chitra Boutique |      2 |     9
           4 | Deepak & Sons   |      0 |     0
           5 | Eshwar Mart     |      2 |    11
           6 | Farah Fashions  |      0 |     0
(6 rows)

### Hands-on

#### Where the filter goes: ON versus WHERE

For an inner join a predicate in ON and the same predicate in WHERE are equivalent. For an outer join they are not. The ON clause decides which rows match; WHERE then filters the already joined result, including the NULL-extended rows. A WHERE predicate on the nullable side therefore discards the unmatched rows and converts the outer join back into an inner join.

blocks.code:
-- Intent: all customers, with their SHIPPED orders where they exist.
-- Filter in ON: outer join preserved.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'SHIPPED'
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Filter in WHERE: unmatched customers are removed.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'SHIPPED'
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

blocks.text:
*customers survive; in WHERE it is applied after the join to rows whose* `status` *is NULL for unmatched customers, so four customers* *are lost.*

When the intent is "customers that have no shipped order", the correct form is an anti-join, not `WHERE o.status <>` `'SHIPPED'`, which is also false for NULL.

#### Joins in Java: JDBC and JPA

A join result is flat, while a Java domain model is a graph. Two designs are common. With JDBC or `JdbcTemplate` a `RowMapper` maps one flat row to one DTO, and a one-to-many join needs a `ResultSetExtractor` that groups consecutive rows by parent key. With JPA, an association such as `Customer.orders` is loaded lazily by default and produces one additional query per customer (the N+1 problem, treated in the query-optimisation chapters); `JOIN` `FETCH` loads parents and children in a single joined query.

blocks.text:
Fetch-joining a collection together with pagination (`Pageable`) is a known defect: Hibernate cannot apply LIMIT to the joined rows, so it fetches everything and paginates in memory, emitting the warning `HHH000104:` `firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory`. The remedy is to page the parent ids first and then fetch the children for those ids.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: revenue totals inflated by a join fan-out

**Scenario.** A finance report computes revenue per customer from order lines and also reports the amount received from the `payments` table, in a single query joining `orders`, `order_items` and `payments`. The revenue column exceeds the real revenue for some customers, and the discrepancy changes when a customer pays in instalments.

**Symptoms.** The report restricts itself to paid and shipped orders. For customer 1 it shows revenue 80,700 and received 120,500, while the ledger shows 77,800 for both; for customer 2 it shows 75,750 and 50,500 against a ledger value of 25,250. Customer 5, whose orders each have one line and one payment, is correct, which hides the defect in tests that use simple data.

**Diagnosis.** Step 1: reproduce the report query.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) AS revenue,
       sum(p.amount)               AS received
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN payments p     ON p.order_id  = o.order_id
WHERE o.status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED')
GROUP BY o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.customer_id;

blocks.text: Step 2: compute each measure separately, with no join between the two child tables.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       (SELECT sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) FROM order_items oi
        JOIN orders o2 ON o2.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
          AND o2.status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED')) AS revenue,
       (SELECT sum(p.amount) FROM payments p
        JOIN orders o3 ON o3.order_id = p.order_id
        WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id) AS received
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) o
ORDER BY o.customer_id;

blocks.text: Revenue and receipts agree with each other and with the ledger (77,800 and 25,250); the report query is therefore wrong, not the data. Step 3: inspect the rows of one order that has several lines and several payments.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.order_id, oi.line_no, oi.qty * oi.unit_price AS line_amount, p.payment_id, p.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN payments p     ON p.order_id  = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 101
ORDER BY oi.line_no, p.payment_id;

blocks.caption: Order 101 has 2 lines and 2 payments. Joining both child tables to the order yields 2 x 2 = 4 rows, so each line amount is counted twice and each payment twice; summing after the join doubles both totals (2900 becomes 5800 and the payments 2900 becomes 5800).
blocks.alt: order_items (order 101) joined rows: 2 x 2 = 4 | line_no amount | line_no line_amt pay_id pay_amt | 1 1500 | 1 1500 1 1000 | 2 1400 | 1 1500 2 1900 | 2 1400 1 1000 | payments (order 101) | 2 1400 2 1900 | pay_id amount | 1 1000 join on order_id | sum(line_amt) = 5800 (true 2900) | 2 1900 | sum(pay_amt) = 5800 (true 2900) | red = value repeated by the join | Fix: aggregate each child table to one row per order first.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The two child tables are both one-to-many from `orders` and are unrelated to each other. Joining them to the same parent produces the product of their row counts per parent (here 2 x 2 for order 101 and 2 x 3 for order 103), and the aggregate then sums every repeated value. Row multiplication after a join is called fan-out. The error does not raise an exception and grows with the data.

**Fix.** Immediate: aggregate each child table to one row per order before joining, so that every input to the join is unique on the join key.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       sum(i.revenue)  AS revenue,
       sum(p.received) AS received
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(qty * unit_price) AS revenue FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i
  ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS received FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p
  ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED')
GROUP BY o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.customer_id;

blocks.text:
Every customer now shows equal revenue and receipts, matching step 2. The permanent fix is to make the grain of each aggregate explicit in the query: each child table is reduced in its own subquery or common table expression, so that every join input is unique on the join key. The outer join to payments keeps orders whose payment has not yet arrived.

**Prevention.** Before joining a table, state its grain (the columns that identify one row) and the grain of the result. If a join target is not unique on the join key, aggregate it first. A reconciliation test that compares the report total with `SELECT sum(...)` on the base table, using data with several lines and several payments per order, detects fan-out. Treat `SELECT DISTINCT` or `count(DISTINCT ...)` added "to fix duplicates" as a defect marker: it hides the multiplication without correcting sums.

#### Incident: customers disappear from a report after a filter is added

**Scenario.** A report lists every customer with the count of shipped orders. A developer adds `AND status = 'SHIPPED'` as a WHERE predicate to an existing LEFT JOIN query. **Symptoms.** Customers with no shipped orders vanish from the report, and the report now shows two customers instead of six. **Diagnosis.** The predicate references the nullable side of an outer join, so rows extended with NULL are discarded (see the hands-on section above: the WHERE form returns two rows, the ON form six). **Fix.** Move the predicate into the ON clause, or compute the count with `count(*) FILTER` `(WHERE o.status = 'SHIPPED')` over an unfiltered left join. **Prevention.** Review rule: in a query with an outer join, every predicate on the optional table belongs in ON; a WHERE predicate on that table is almost always a defect unless it is `IS NULL` (anti-join).

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN? INNER JOIN returns only pairs that satisfy the condition. LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left table, with NULL in the right-hand columns where no match exists. Choosing the wrong one silently drops or keeps rows; an outer join is required whenever the report must show entities with no related rows.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does a WHERE condition on the right table change the meaning of a LEFT JOIN? WHERE is evaluated after the join. Unmatched left rows carry NULL in right-table columns, so a predicate such as `o.status = 'SHIPPED'` is not true for them and they are removed. The join then behaves as an inner join. The predicate belongs in ON when it should only restrict the matching.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How is a semi-join different from an inner join? A semi-join (EXISTS or IN) returns each left row at most once if any match exists and returns no right-hand columns. An inner join returns one row per matching pair, so a left row with several matches is repeated. Semi-joins are the correct tool for "has at least one".

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Name three ways to find rows with no match and compare them. NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN with IS NULL on the right primary key, and NOT IN. NOT EXISTS and the left join are null-safe and usually produce the same anti-join plan in PostgreSQL. NOT IN returns no rows at all when the subquery contains a NULL, and is also harder for the planner to optimise.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Describe join fan-out and how it is prevented. When two unrelated one-to-many tables are joined to the same parent, rows multiply per parent and sums are inflated. Prevention is to aggregate each many-side table to the grain of the join key before joining, or to compute each measure in a separate subquery.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Which join algorithms exist and when does the planner choose each? Nested loop (few outer rows, indexed inner side), hash join (large inputs, equality), merge join (sorted inputs or large inputs with equality). The choice is cost-based from the statistics; `EXPLAIN` shows it.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How is a FULL OUTER JOIN written in MySQL? MySQL has no FULL JOIN. A left join combined with a right join through `UNION` gives the same result; `UNION ALL` of a left join and an anti-join avoids the duplicate-removal step.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Joins

- A join is a filtered Cartesian product; the join type decides the fate of unmatched rows.
- Predicates on the optional side of an outer join belong in ON; in WHERE they turn the join into an inner join.
- Semi-joins (EXISTS) and anti-joins (NOT EXISTS) answer "has any" and "has none" without duplicating rows.
- Joining two unrelated one-to-many tables to one parent multiplies rows; aggregate each child table first.
- Know the grain of every input: a non-unique join key is the root of duplicates.
- JPA lazy associations cause N+1 queries; JOIN FETCH fixes it but must not be combined with pagination of the parent.

An aggregate function reduces a set of rows to one value: a count, a sum, an average, a minimum. Combined with GROUP BY, the reduction is performed once per group, which turns a table of events into a table of metrics. Nearly every dashboard, report and reconciliation query is an aggregation. The defects found in them have a small number of causes: NULL values that aggregates skip silently, groups formed on the wrong columns, filters applied at the wrong stage and rows that were multiplied before aggregation (see the join chapter).

### Concept and mechanism

#### Aggregate functions and their treatment of NULL

An aggregate ignores NULL inputs, with one exception: `count(*)` counts rows and does not look at any column. If every input is NULL, or the group has no rows, the result is NULL for every aggregate except `count`, which returns 0.

rows: Number of rows in the group
Number of rows where expr is not NULL
Total and mean of the non-NULL values
Skips NULL; NULL if no input
Smallest and largest value, any ordered type
Logical AND / OR over booleans (PostgreSQL; MySQL uses MIN/MAX of 0/1)
Array of the values (PostgreSQL only; MySQL: JSON\_ARRAYAGG)
blocks.caption: Common aggregate functions.

blocks.text: The result types matter in Java. In PostgreSQL `count` returns `bigint` (a Java `long`), `sum(integer)` returns `bigint`, `sum(bigint)` and `sum(numeric)` return `numeric` (a `BigDecimal`), and `avg` of an integer type returns `numeric`. Reading `count(*)` into an `int` field with an unchecked cast, or comparing a `Long` with `==`, are common faults.

blocks.code:
SELECT count(*)                AS all_rows,
       count(dept_id)          AS with_dept,
       count(DISTINCT dept_id) AS distinct_depts,
       sum(salary)             AS payroll,
       avg(salary)::numeric(10,2) AS mean_salary,
       min(hire_date)          AS first_hire
FROM employees;

blocks.text:
Fourteen rows exist, but `count(dept_id)` is 13 because employee 13 has no department, and `count(DISTINCT` `dept_id)` is 4 because the employees reference four departments (department 50, Legal, has no employee).

#### How GROUP BY works

GROUP BY partitions the rows that survive WHERE into groups of rows with equal values in the grouping expressions, then evaluates each aggregate once per group. For grouping purposes NULLs are treated as equal to each other, so all NULLs of a grouping column form one group (unlike in a comparison, where NULL is never equal to NULL). Every column in the SELECT list must be a grouping expression, an aggregate, or functionally dependent on the grouping columns (a column of a table whose primary key is grouped).

The server forms the groups in one of two ways. A hash aggregate builds an in-memory hash table keyed by the grouping columns and updates the aggregate state as rows stream past; it needs no sorted input but needs memory proportional to the number of groups. A group aggregate requires the input sorted on the grouping columns (by an explicit sort or an index) and emits a group whenever the key changes; it needs almost no memory. EXPLAIN shows `HashAggregate` or `GroupAggregate`.

blocks.code:
SELECT dept_id, count(*) AS n, sum(salary) AS payroll, round(avg(salary)) AS mean
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id NULLS LAST;

blocks.text: The NULL group is shown last: employee 13 forms a group of its own. A frequent request, "employees per department including empty departments", cannot be answered from `employees` alone; it needs a left join from `departments` and `count(e.emp_id)`, not `count(*)`, because an empty department still yields one joined row.

SELECT d.dept_name, count(*) AS wrong, count(e.emp_id) AS right
FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_name;

dept_name  | wrong | right
-------------+-------+-------
 Engineering |     5 |     5
 Finance     |     2 |     2
 HR          |     2 |     2
 Legal       |     1 |     0
 Sales       |     4 |     4
(5 rows)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
Legal shows 1 with `count(*)` and 0 with `count(e.emp_id)`. The NULL-extended row produced by the outer join is a row, and `count(*)` counts it.

#### The standard rule and MySQL's ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY

A SELECT list item that is neither grouped nor aggregated is an error in PostgreSQL. MySQL has the same rule under the SQL mode `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` (enabled by default since 5.7.5) and detects functional dependence on the primary key; with the mode off it returns an arbitrary row's value, which produces plausible but wrong results.

blocks.code: SELECT dept_id, first_name, max(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;

ERROR:  column "employees.first_name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate
        function
LINE 1: SELECT dept_id, first_name, max(salary) FROM employees GROUP...
                        ^
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
PostgreSQL does accept `SELECT d.dept_name, count(*) FROM departments d JOIN employees e USING (dept_id)` `GROUP BY d.dept_id` because `dept_name` is functionally dependent on the grouped primary key `d.dept_id`.

### Filtering aggregates: HAVING and FILTER

HAVING filters groups, WHERE filters rows. A condition that does not involve an aggregate must be placed in WHERE, because it then reduces the work done before grouping. The conditional aggregate clause `FILTER (WHERE ...)` (PostgreSQL 9.4 and later, SQLite 3.30 and later, not in MySQL) restricts the rows that feed one aggregate and allows several differently filtered aggregates in a single pass; the portable form is `sum(CASE WHEN cond THEN x END)`, which works because CASE without ELSE yields NULL and aggregates skip NULL.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name,
       count(*)                                         AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'PAID')        AS paid,
       count(CASE WHEN o.status = 'NEW' THEN 1 END)     AS new_portable
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING count(*) >= 2
ORDER BY c.name;

name       | orders | paid | new_portable
-----------------+--------+------+--------------
 Anil Traders    |      3 |    2 |            0
 Bharat Stores   |      3 |    1 |            1
 Chitra Boutique |      2 |    1 |            1
 Eshwar Mart     |      2 |    1 |            0
(4 rows)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
The two conditional forms are equivalent; the FILTER form reads more clearly and cannot be broken by a missing ELSE. This technique is also the standard way to pivot rows into columns, used in the interview problems at the end of this part.

### Multiple levels of aggregation: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE

Reports often require totals at several levels in one result: per department, per location and overall. Three clauses generate them from a single scan. `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())` lists the groupings explicitly. `ROLLUP (a, b)` is shorthand for `((a, b), (a), ())`, the hierarchy of subtotals. `CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for every subset: `((a, b),` `(a), (b), ())`. In rows produced for a coarser grouping the omitted columns are NULL, which is indistinguishable from a real NULL value; the function `GROUPING(col)` returns 1 when the column was rolled up and 0 otherwise.

blocks.alt: blue path = ROLLUP; orange branch added by CUBE rows returned | (location, dept_name) | GROUP BY ROLLUP (location, dept_name) | 4 rows | 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 | GROUP BY CUBE (location, dept_name) | 4 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 12 | (location) (dept_name) | 3 rows 4 rows | GROUPING SETS ((location), (dept_name)) | 3 + 4 = 7 | GROUP BY location, dept_name | () grand total 4 | 1 row

blocks.code:
SELECT d.location, d.dept_name, count(*) AS n, sum(e.salary) AS payroll,
       GROUPING(d.location) AS g_loc, GROUPING(d.dept_name) AS g_dept
FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (d.location, d.dept_name)
ORDER BY d.location NULLS LAST, d.dept_name NULLS LAST;

blocks.text: Rows with `g_dept = 1` are the location subtotals and the row with both flags set is the grand total. Without `GROUPING` the application cannot tell a subtotal row from a department with a NULL name. MySQL supports only `GROUP BY a, b` `WITH ROLLUP`, with `GROUPING()` available since 8.0.1; it has no `GROUPING SETS` or `CUBE`, so those require `UNION ALL` of several GROUP BY queries, scanning the table once per grouping.

### String and array aggregation

`string_agg(expr, delimiter ORDER BY ...)` concatenates the values of a group. MySQL's equivalent is `GROUP_CONCAT(expr ORDER BY ... SEPARATOR ',')`. PostgreSQL places the ordering inside the aggregate call; without it the order of concatenation is undefined, as for any unordered set of rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT d.dept_name,
       string_agg(e.first_name, ', ' ORDER BY e.first_name) AS members,
       array_agg(e.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id) AS ids
FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_name ORDER BY d.dept_name;

blocks.title: Result

blocks.text: The Legal row shows the difference in NULL handling: `string_agg` skips the NULL produced by the outer join and returns NULL, whereas `array_agg` keeps it and returns `{NULL}`, an array with one element.

headers: MySQL 8.x (not run on the build machine)
blocks.caption: Concatenating aggregates.

blocks.text:
The MySQL truncation produces a result that looks valid and is incomplete; it generates a warning (code 1260) that most clients and drivers do not surface.

### Worked example: a per-department salary report

Requirement: for each department with at least two employees, the payroll, the highest salary, and the share of the company payroll, ordered by share.

The statement and its result are printed after the trace.

1. FROM and JOIN produce 13 rows (employee 13 has no department).
2. GROUP BY `dept_name` forms four groups: Engineering (5 rows, payroll 850000), Sales (4, 485000), HR (2, 220000) and Finance (2, 250000).
3. HAVING keeps groups with two or more rows; all four qualify.
4. The select-list expression `sum(sum(e.salary)) OVER ()` first computes `sum(e.salary)` per group, then applies a window function over the grouped result: the grand total of the four payrolls, 1,805,000. A window function operates after aggregation; the window chapter explains the mechanics.
5. The percentages are 850000 / 1805000 = 47.1 for Engineering, and so on.

blocks.code:
SELECT d.dept_name,
       count(*)                                           AS headcount,
       sum(e.salary)                                      AS payroll,
       max(e.salary)                                      AS top_salary,
       round(100 * sum(e.salary) / sum(sum(e.salary)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_name
HAVING count(*) >= 2
ORDER BY pct DESC;

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

Aggregation over Java data access typically returns either an array row or a projection. Spring Data JPA maps a grouped query to an interface projection:

blocks.title: DeptStats.java (fragment; not run)

blocks.text:
Performance of aggregation is governed by the amount of data scanned, not by the result size: `count(*)` on a large table reads the whole table (or a whole index) in PostgreSQL, because row visibility must be checked under MVCC. The query-optimisation chapters treat this and the alternatives (approximate counts, summary tables, partial indexes).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: customers-per-city dashboard does not add up

**Scenario.** A dashboard shows the number of customers per city using `SELECT city, count(city) FROM customers` `GROUP BY city`. The management total of customers is 6, but the dashboard figures add up to 5, and one row shows a city with an empty label and a count of 0.

**Symptoms.** The dashboard has a row without a name and a zero count, and the column sums disagree with `SELECT` `count(*) FROM customers`.

**Diagnosis.** Step 1: compare the grouped counts with the total.

blocks.code:
city    | counted | rows_in_group
-----------+---------+---------------
 Chennai   |       1 |             1
 Delhi     |       1 |             1
 Hyderabad |       2 |             2
 Mumbai    |       1 |             1
           |       0 |             1
(5 rows)

 total | with_city
-------+-----------
     6 |         5
(1 row)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
The first query shows a group with `city` NULL: the grouping step keeps customer 4 (city unknown) as a group, but `count(city)` counts only non-NULL values of the grouped column, which for that group is none. The second query confirms the discrepancy: 6 rows against 5 non-NULL cities.

**Root cause.** `count(column)` skips NULL by definition. Applied to the grouping column itself it returns 0 for the NULL group. The same rule underlies other silently wrong metrics: `avg(col)` divides by the number of non-NULL values, so averages over a sparse column describe only the rows that have a value.

**Fix.** Immediate: use `count(*)` for "number of rows" and label the NULL group explicitly with `coalesce(city,` `'Unknown')`. Permanent: decide per metric what a missing value means (excluded, zero, or its own category) and encode that decision in the query: `avg(coalesce(x, 0))` for "missing means zero", `avg(x)` for "average of known values".

blocks.code:
SELECT coalesce(city, 'Unknown') AS city, count(*) AS customers
FROM customers GROUP BY coalesce(city, 'Unknown') ORDER BY 1;

city    | customers
-----------+-----------
 Chennai   |         1
 Delhi     |         1
 Hyderabad |         2
 Mumbai    |         1
 Unknown   |         1
(5 rows)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Reconcile every grouped report against an ungrouped total (`sum` of the groups equals the total). Add NOT NULL constraints to columns whose absence is not meaningful so that the question does not arise.

#### Incident: truncated group_concat in MySQL (typical)

**Scenario.** A MySQL-backed export builds a comma-separated list of tag identifiers per article with `GROUP_CONCAT(tag_id)`. Articles with many tags are exported with a cut-off list. **Diagnosis.** `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE` `'group_concat_max_len'` returns 1024 (the default), and `SHOW WARNINGS` after the query contains `Warning 1260 Row 3` `was cut by GROUP_CONCAT()`. **Fix.** `SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = 1048576;` before the query or set it in the server configuration; prefer `JSON_ARRAYAGG` and let the application decode the array. **Prevention.** Treat warnings from the driver as errors in tests, and avoid delivering data as one concatenated string.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between `count(*)`, `count(column)` and `count(DISTINCT column)`? `count(*)` counts rows. `count(column)` counts rows where the column is not NULL. `count(DISTINCT column)` counts distinct non-NULL values. A table with 14 rows, 13 non-NULL department ids of which 4 distinct values are used returns 14, 13 and 4.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why can a SELECT list not contain a column that is absent from GROUP BY? Each group yields one output row, so a non-grouped column would have several candidate values. The standard requires the column to be grouped, aggregated, or functionally dependent on grouped columns (such as a column of a table whose primary key is grouped). MySQL with ONLY\_FULL\_GROUP\_BY applies the same rule; without that mode it returns an arbitrary value.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Where does a filter belong, in WHERE or in HAVING? A condition on individual rows belongs in WHERE: it reduces the rows before grouping. A condition on an aggregate belongs in HAVING because the aggregate exists only after grouping. Putting a row condition in HAVING gives the same result but does unnecessary work.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How can several differently filtered counts be computed in one query? With conditional aggregation: `count(*) FILTER` `(WHERE status = 'PAID')` in PostgreSQL or `sum(CASE WHEN status = 'PAID' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` in any engine. One pass over the data computes all of them.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What do ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS do? They compute aggregates at several grouping levels in one statement. ROLLUP produces the hierarchy of subtotals ending in a grand total, CUBE every combination of the columns and GROUPING SETS exactly the listed combinations. `GROUPING()` distinguishes a subtotal NULL from a data NULL. MySQL supports only `WITH ROLLUP`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do NULLs behave in GROUP BY and in aggregates? NULLs form a single group in GROUP BY, although NULL = NULL is not true in comparisons. Aggregates other than `count(*)` skip NULL inputs, and return NULL when no non-NULL input exists (`count` returns 0).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What do HashAggregate and GroupAggregate mean in a plan? HashAggregate builds a hash table of groups and needs memory proportional to the number of groups. GroupAggregate consumes input sorted on the grouping keys and needs little memory. The planner chooses by estimated group count and by whether sorted input (an index) is available.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Aggregation and grouping

- Aggregates skip NULL; only `count(*)` counts rows. Choose count variants deliberately.
- GROUP BY forms one group for all NULLs; non-grouped columns in SELECT are an error unless functionally dependent.
- WHERE reduces rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after aggregation; FILTER or CASE gives several conditional aggregates in one pass.
- ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS replace several UNION ALL queries; use GROUPING() to identify subtotal rows.
- The grain of the input decides the correctness of every sum; reconcile each report against an ungrouped total.
- Java side: `count` maps to `long`, `sum(numeric)` to `BigDecimal`.

A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement. A common table expression (CTE), introduced with `WITH`, gives a name to a subquery so that it can be referenced like a table, can be referenced more than once, and, in its recursive form, can walk hierarchies and graphs. Both constructs express logic that a single flat join cannot: "employees paid above their department average", "customers with no orders", "the latest order of each customer", "all subordinates of a manager at any depth". They are also the source of two of the most common production defects, the NOT IN trap and the correlated subquery executed once per outer row.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Where a subquery may appear

rows: One row, one column; usable wherever an expression is
Several rows, one column; used with IN, ANY, ALL, EXISTS
Any shape; used in FROM with an alias
References a column of the outer query; logically executed once per outer row
`WHERE salary > (SELECT` `avg(salary) FROM employees x` `WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id)`
blocks.caption: Kinds of subquery.

blocks.text: A scalar subquery that returns more than one row is a run-time error in PostgreSQL ("more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression"). MySQL raises error 1242 ("Subquery returns more than 1 row"). A scalar subquery that returns no row yields NULL.

blocks.code:
emp_id | first_name |    dept
--------+------------+-------------
      1 | Asha       | Engineering
     13 | Tara       |
(2 rows)

ERROR:  more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
#### Correlated subqueries

An uncorrelated subquery is independent of the outer query and is evaluated once. A correlated subquery refers to the outer row, so its result changes per row. The standard example compares each employee with the average of the employee's own department.

blocks.code:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT avg(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id)
ORDER BY e.dept_id, e.salary DESC;

blocks.text: Logically the inner query runs once for each of the 14 outer rows. Physically the planner may execute it exactly like that (a `SubPlan` node evaluated per row), or, for the forms it can transform (EXISTS, IN, NOT EXISTS, ANY), convert it into a join. Scalar correlated subqueries in the SELECT list or with an aggregate are normally not transformed by PostgreSQL, which is the source of the performance incident described below. The equivalent rewrite computes each department average once and joins to it:

blocks.code:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, avg(salary) AS avg_sal FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) a
  ON a.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > a.avg_sal
ORDER BY e.dept_id, e.salary DESC;

blocks.text:
Employee 13 (no department) never appears in either form: the comparison with the average of an empty or NULL-keyed group is not true.

#### EXISTS, IN and JOIN

Three constructs answer "rows of A that have a matching row in B". They differ in duplicate handling and in NULL behaviour.

rows: Correct for any "has a match" test
Same plan as EXISTS in PostgreSQL
Must be de-duplicated if only A is wanted
One NULL makes the result empty
blocks.caption: EXISTS, IN and JOIN compared.

blocks.text:
In current PostgreSQL versions `EXISTS` and `IN` over an uncorrelated or simply correlated subquery are planned as the same semi-join, so the choice is one of readability. This was not true historically for MySQL, where `IN (subquery)` was executed as a dependent subquery before 5.6 and is optimised by semi-join strategies from 5.6 onwards. `NOT IN` is not equivalent to `NOT EXISTS`, as the first incident below shows.

#### Common table expressions

`WITH name AS (subquery) SELECT ...` defines one or more named result sets visible in the main statement. A CTE improves readability, lets a result be used twice and structures multi-step logic. Since PostgreSQL 12 a non-recursive CTE that is referenced once and has no side effects is inlined like a subquery, so the planner can push predicates into it; one referenced several times is computed once and materialised. The keywords `MATERIALIZED` and `NOT MATERIALIZED` override the choice. Before version 12 every CTE was an optimisation fence, and many old queries were written (or rewritten) with that behaviour in mind. MySQL 8.0 merges CTEs into the outer query when possible and materialises them otherwise.
CTEs may also contain data-modifying statements (PostgreSQL), which allows delete-and-archive in one atomic statement:

blocks.code:
INSERT 0 2
 payments_left | archived
---------------+----------
             8 |        2
(1 row)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
### Recursive CTEs and hierarchies

A recursive CTE has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`: an anchor query that produces the starting rows and a recursive query that references the CTE itself. The engine evaluates it iteratively: the anchor result becomes the working table; the recursive query is run against the working table; its output is appended to the result and becomes the next working table; evaluation stops when an iteration produces no rows. The algorithm terminates only when the data is finite and acyclic, or when the query contains its own stopping condition.

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT emp_id, first_name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, first_name::text AS path
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL                    -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1,
         o.path || ' > ' || e.first_name
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id     -- recursive step
)
SELECT emp_id, depth, path FROM org ORDER BY path;

blocks.text:
**anchor (depth 0)** `1`

**iteration 1 (depth 1)** `2 6 9 11 13` \<- managed by rows of the previous table

**iteration 2 (depth 2)** `3 4 7 8 10 12 14` \<- managed by rows of the previous table

**iteration 3 (depth 3)** `5` \<- managed by rows of the previous table

**iteration 4** empty: recursion stops

**rows produced: 1 + 5 + 7 + 1 = 14**

*Figure 1.38. The working table of the recursive CTE over* `employees`*, iteration by iteration. Each iteration finds the employees whose* *manager is in the previous working table; the iteration after depth 3 returns no row and evaluation stops after producing 14 rows in* *total.*

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT emp_id, first_name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, first_name::text AS path
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1,
         o.path || ' > ' || e.first_name
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id
)
SELECT emp_id, depth, path FROM org ORDER BY path;

emp_id | depth |             path
--------+-------+-------------------------------
      1 |     0 | Asha
      6 |     1 | Asha > Arjun
      8 |     2 | Asha > Arjun > Kiran
     14 |     2 | Asha > Arjun > Omar
      7 |     2 | Asha > Arjun > Priya
      9 |     1 | Asha > Divya
     10 |     2 | Asha > Divya > Rahul
     11 |     1 | Asha > Neha
     12 |     2 | Asha > Neha > Sanjay
     13 |     1 | Asha > Tara

      3 |     2 | Asha > Vikram > Meera
      5 |     3 | Asha > Vikram > Meera > Sneha

blocks.text:
The recursion supports "all subordinates of manager 6" (anchor `WHERE emp_id = 6`), "the chain of managers above an employee" (follow `manager_id` upward) and bill-of-materials explosions. Cycles in the data (employee A manages B and B manages A) make the recursion run forever. Defences are a depth limit in the recursive step (`WHERE o.depth < 20`), `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` (which removes already-seen rows, though only when entire rows match, so a changing `depth` or `path` column defeats it) and the PostgreSQL 14 clause `CYCLE emp_id SET is_cycle USING cycle_path`. MySQL 8 supports `WITH RECURSIVE`, limits recursion by `cte_max_recursion_depth` (default 1000) and has no `CYCLE` or `SEARCH` clause.

### LATERAL subqueries

A `LATERAL` subquery in FROM may reference columns of the tables that precede it, which makes it a per-row function returning a table. The classic use is "top N rows of a child table for each parent", which a plain join cannot express because LIMIT applies to the whole result. PostgreSQL has supported it since 9.3, MySQL since 8.0.14 (as `JOIN` `LATERAL`), and SQL Server offers `CROSS APPLY`.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, r.order_id, r.order_ts::date AS day, r.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.order_ts, o.status
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    ORDER BY o.order_ts DESC
    LIMIT 2
) r ON true
ORDER BY c.customer_id, r.order_ts DESC;

### Worked example: employees above their department average

The statement `SELECT ... WHERE salary > (SELECT avg(...) ... WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id)` is traced on the sample data.

1. For employee 1 the inner query binds `e.dept_id = 10` and computes the average of the Engineering salaries 250000, 180000, 150000, 150000 and 120000, which is 170000. The comparison 250000 \> 170000 is true; the row is kept.
2. Employee 2 (180000) is compared with the same average of 170000: true.
3. Employees 3 and 4 (150000) and employee 5 (120000) are below 170000: false.
4. For Sales (employees 6, 7, 8 and 14; salaries 170000, 110000, 95000 and 110000) the average is 121250. Only employee 6 (170000) exceeds it.
5. For employee 13 the inner query binds `e.dept_id = NULL`; `x.dept_id = NULL` is never true, so the inner query sees no rows, `avg` returns NULL, and `salary > NULL` is unknown: the row is dropped.

The result shown earlier confirms the trace: Engineering contributes employees 1 and 2, Sales contributes employee 6, and employees 9 and 11 qualify because each is the better paid of two in a department whose average lies between the two salaries.

### Hands-on

The three formulations of an anti-join (`NOT EXISTS`, `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`, `NOT IN`) produce visibly different plans. The experiment uses `big_customers` (2,000 rows) and `big_orders` (200,000 rows) loaded for the examples in this chapter.

QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Hash Right Anti Join
         Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
         ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o
         ->  Hash
               ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c
(6 rows)

                QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c
         Filter: (NOT (hashed SubPlan 1))
         SubPlan 1
           ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o
(5 rows)

blocks.text:
`NOT EXISTS` becomes a hash anti join (`Hash Right Anti Join`, with the larger table as the probe side), an efficient single pass. `NOT IN` becomes a filter on a hashed `SubPlan` because the planner must preserve the NULL semantics: it cannot turn the construct into an anti-join unless it can prove the subquery column is never NULL. The first plan is therefore preferable on large tables, in addition to being semantically safer.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: NOT IN returns no rows because of a NULL

**Scenario.** A clean-up job lists departments without employees with `SELECT dept_name FROM departments WHERE` `dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)`. Legal has no employees, yet the job reports that all departments have staff.

**Symptoms.** The query returns zero rows although `departments` contains a department that no employee references. The result was correct in the development database and became empty after a contractor without a department was added in production.

**Diagnosis.** Step 1: run the query and the same query with the subquery restricted to non-NULL values.

-----------
(0 rows)

-----------

(1 row)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text: Step 2: confirm that the subquery returns a NULL.

**Root cause.** `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` is evaluated as `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`. The last term is unknown for every `x`, so the whole conjunction can be at best unknown and never true. A WHERE clause keeps only true rows, so none survives. The behaviour is correct three-valued logic, not a defect of the database.

**50 NOT IN (10, 20, 30, 40, NULL) = 50 \<\> 10 AND 50 \<\> 20 AND 50 \<\> 30 AND 50 \<\> 40 AND 50 \<\> NULL**

**50 \<\> 10 50 \<\> 20 50 \<\> 30 50 \<\> 40 50 \<\> NULL** AND AND AND AND **TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE UNKNOWN**

NOT EXISTS or TRUE AND TRUE AND TRUE AND TRUE AND UNKNOWN IS NOT NULL filter: TRUE, row kept

**= UNKNOWN: WHERE rejects the row**

*Figure 1.40. Evaluation of* `50 NOT IN (10, 20, 30, 40, NULL)`*. Each comparison with a real value is true, but the comparison* *with NULL is unknown and the AND of true and unknown is unknown, so the row is rejected. With the NULL removed, or with NOT* *EXISTS, the result is true.*

**Fix.** Immediate: rewrite as an anti-join that is not sensitive to NULL.

Permanent: use `NOT EXISTS` for every "has no matching row" test, in SQL, JPQL and Criteria queries; make columns that must be present `NOT NULL`, so that the question cannot arise. **Prevention.** A test with a NULL in the subquery column is part of the standard test data; static review flags every `NOT IN (SELECT ...)`. Note that `NOT IN` over a literal list from application code has the same behaviour when the list contains a null element.

#### Incident: slow report caused by a correlated subquery

**Scenario.** A nightly report lists every customer with total spend on orders that are not in status NEW. The query uses a scalar subquery in the SELECT list. It ran in well under a second with 20 test customers and takes minutes in production, where `big_customers` has 2,000 rows and `big_orders` 200,000.

**Symptoms.** The query's run time grows with the product of customers and orders; CPU is saturated and `pg_stat_activity` shows one backend running for minutes; adding more memory does not help.

**Diagnosis.** Step 1: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a sample of 100 customers.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY ON)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       (SELECT sum(o.amount) FROM big_orders o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status <> 'NEW') AS spend
FROM big_customers c WHERE c.customer_id <= 100;

QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Index Only Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c (actual rows=100 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (customer_id <= 100)
   Heap Fetches: 100
   SubPlan 1
     ->  Aggregate (actual rows=1 loops=100)
           ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=80 loops=100)
                 Filter: ((status <> 'NEW'::text) AND (customer_id = c.customer_id))
                 Rows Removed by Filter: 199920
 Planning Time: 0.889 ms
 Execution Time: 1350.645 ms
(10 rows)
blocks.title: Result

blocks.text:
The plan shows a `SubPlan` with `loops=100`: the inner `Seq Scan on big_orders` is executed once per customer and removes 199,920 rows each time (reading all 200,000 rows to keep 80). The whole statement costs 100 full scans (about 1.5 s in the run shown; runs on the same machine varied between 1.5 and 4 s, because other processes share it); the 2,000-customer report therefore needs 20 times as many scans, and the time grows linearly with both table sizes. All timings are measured on the build machine and are typical, not exact.

**Root cause.** A correlated scalar subquery with an aggregate is executed per outer row, and no index exists on `big_orders(customer_id)` to make each execution cheap. The planner cannot unnest this form into a join.

**Fix.** Immediate: aggregate once and join.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY ON)
SELECT c.customer_id, s.spend
FROM big_customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS spend
           FROM big_orders WHERE status <> 'NEW'
           GROUP BY customer_id) s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id <= 100;

               Workers Launched: 1
