blocks.text: Three remedies exist, and the right one depends on the use case:

blocks.title: OrderRepository.java (fragment, unverified)

blocks.text:
The third is batch fetching: `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50` (or `@BatchSize(size` `= 50)` on the association) makes Hibernate load the lazy customers of 50 orders with a single `where c.id in (?, ?,` `...)`, reducing 51 statements to 2 without changing the queries. A fetch join combined with a `Pageable` on a *collection* association (one-to-many) produces the warning `firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch;` `applying in memory`, because the join multiplies rows; use batch fetching or a two-step query for collections. A projection that selects only the needed columns (`select o.id, c.name from Order o join o.customer c`) avoids loading entities at all.

### Worked example

#### Rewriting a correlated subquery

A report lists every customer with the number of December orders. The first version uses a correlated subquery:

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o
         WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2024-12-01') AS dec_orders
FROM customers c;

blocks.text: Step 1: the plan executes the subquery once for each of the 100 000 customers (`loops=100000`) as a bitmap scan of `idx_orders_customer`, which reads about 15 rows per call and discards 14 of them by the date filter.

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
 Seq Scan on customers c  (actual rows=100000 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=300196 read=1500738 written=16
   SubPlan 1
     ->  Aggregate  (actual rows=1 loops=100000)
           ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (actual rows=1 loops=100000)
                 Recheck Cond: (customer_id = c.id)
                 Filter: (created_at >= '2024-12-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)
                 Rows Removed by Filter: 14
                 Heap Blocks: exact=1500000
 Execution Time: 14732.559 ms
blocks.title: Plan of the correlated version (real, trimmed)

blocks.text: Step 2: count the work: 1.8 million buffers (the sum of hit and read) to produce a result that needs only the 52 801 December orders. Step 3: invert the logic. Aggregate the December orders once, then join:

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, COALESCE(x.n, 0) AS dec_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2024-12-01'
           GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.id;

$ psql -d shop
 Hash Left Join  (actual rows=100000 loops=1)
   Hash Cond: (c.id = x.customer_id)
   ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (actual rows=100000 loops=1)
   ->  Hash  (actual rows=52801 loops=1)
         ->  HashAggregate  (actual rows=52801 loops=1)
               ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created on orders  (actual rows=52801 loops=1)
                     Index Cond: (created_at >= '2024-12-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)
 Execution Time: 63.894 ms
blocks.title: Plan of the rewritten version (real, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The execution time dropped from 14 733 ms to 64 ms (230 times) and the buffers from 1.8 million to about 1600. The change is not magic: the first plan touched each of the 1.5 million orders through a per-customer index lookup; the second touched only the 52 801 relevant orders, once, in index order. The general principle is to make the filter that removes most data run first and once.

### Hands-on

Each technique below has a before and after that can be repeated on the `orders` table.

#### 1. Function on an indexed column

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
 Aggregate  (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..43334.00 rows=7500 width=0) (actual rows=4320 loops=1)
         Filter: (date(created_at) = '2024-06-01'::date)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 1495680
         Buffers: shared hit=416 read=20418
 Execution Time: 351.006 ms

 Aggregate  (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_created on orders  (actual rows=4320 loops=1)
         Heap Fetches: 0
         Buffers: shared hit=1 read=14
 Execution Time: 0.602 ms
blocks.title: Before and after (real, trimmed)

blocks.text:
If the function must be kept, index the expression. For a `timestamptz` column `date(created_at)` is not immutable (it depends on the session time zone), and `CREATE INDEX ... ((date(created_at)))` fails with `functions in index` `expression must be marked IMMUTABLE`. Fix the zone: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (((created_at AT TIME ZONE` `'UTC')::date))` and query with the identical expression, which produced a bitmap scan of 67 buffers.

#### 2. Implicit cast

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242::numeric;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242::bigint;

$ psql -d shop
 Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..43334.00 rows=7500 width=77) (actual rows=15 loops=1)
   Filter: ((customer_id)::numeric = '4242'::numeric)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 1499985
 Execution Time: 548.670 ms

 Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=4.54..63.52 rows=15 width=77) (actual rows=15 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (customer_id = '4242'::bigint)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_orders_customer  (actual rows=15 loops=1)
 Execution Time: 0.191 ms
blocks.title: Before and after (real, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The visible clue is `(customer_id)::numeric` in the `Filter` line: a cast on the column side. `integer = bigint` is resolved inside the same operator family, so it keeps the index; `integer = numeric` and `integer = text` do not.

#### 3. Pattern matching

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
 Index Scan using idx_cust_email_pat on customers  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=10 width=42)
   (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   Index Cond: ((email ~>=~ 'user77777@'::text) AND (email ~<~ 'user77777A'::text))
   Filter: (email ~~ 'user77777@%'::text)
blocks.title: Plan (real)

blocks.text:
A B-tree can serve `LIKE 'abc%'` only if the index sorts by character values, which requires the `C` collation or the operator class `text_pattern_ops` (or `varchar_pattern_ops`); in the experiment the database collation was `C.UTF-8`, and a plain index on `email` still produced a `Seq Scan` for `LIKE 'user77777@%'`; only the `text_pattern_ops` index was used. A pattern with a leading wildcard needs a trigram index, shown in the incident below. MySQL can use a standard B+tree index for `LIKE 'abc%'` under the usual collations.

#### 4. OR and UNION

`WHERE customer_id = 4242 OR created_at < '2024-01-01 00:10'` was answered by a `BitmapOr` of two indexes (0.1 ms). The same query with `OR note = 'order note xyz'`, where `note` has no index, falls back to a sequential scan of the whole table, because one unindexed branch forces the scan. Either add the missing index or rewrite as `UNION ALL` of two queries when the branches are disjoint (use `UNION` otherwise to remove duplicates).

#### 5. Pagination

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
 Limit  (actual rows=20 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_id on orders  (actual rows=1000020 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared hit=5 read=17719 written=5257
 Execution Time: 463.003 ms

 Limit  (actual rows=20 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created_id on orders  (actual rows=20 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (ROW(created_at, id) > ROW('2024-08-19 11:33:20+00'::timestamptz, 1000000))
         Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1
 Execution Time: 0.054 ms
blocks.title: Plans (real, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The row-value comparison `(created_at, id) > (a, b)` is the SQL-standard way to express a lexicographic condition; PostgreSQL turns it into an index condition on both columns. MySQL 8.0 supports row constructors but may not use the index for them as effectively, so the equivalent expanded form `created_at > ? OR (created_at = ? AND id > ?)` is used there.

#### 6. COUNT(*)

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimate FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders';

$ psql -d shop
 Aggregate  (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Index Only Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders  (actual rows=1500000 loops=1)
         Heap Fetches: 0
         Buffers: shared hit=1 read=1590
 Execution Time: 248.396 ms

 estimate
----------
  1500000
blocks.title: Output (real)

blocks.text:
Counting is linear in table size. When an approximate figure suffices (for example "about 1.5 million results" in a search page), read `reltuples`; for an exact count that is requested often, maintain it in a summary table.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident 7: a function on an indexed column causes a full table scan

**Scenario.** The daily revenue endpoint of an order service filters with `WHERE date(created_at) = :day`. It was written when the table had 50 000 rows and has an index on `created_at`. At 1.5 million rows it takes 350 ms and the database CPU rises with concurrent users.

**Symptoms.** The query is slow although `\d orders` shows an index on `created_at`; `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` for that index does not increase.

**Diagnosis.**

blocks.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE date(created_at) = '2024-06-01';

blocks.text:
The plan (shown above) is a `Seq Scan` with `Filter: (date(created_at) = '2024-06-01'::date)` and `Rows Removed` `by Filter: 1495680`: 1 495 680 rows read to find 4320.

**Root cause.** The function is applied to the column, so the planner cannot map the condition onto the index order. The estimate (7500 rows) also shows that it used a default guess for the function result.

**Fix.** Rewrite as a half-open range on the bare column (`created_at >= :day AND created_at < :day + 1`): 0.6 ms with an index-only scan, 580 times faster. In Spring Data use `findByCreatedAtGreaterThanEqualAndCreatedAtLessThan(start, end)` with `Instant` or `OffsetDateTime` bounds computed in the application's business time zone. If rewriting is impossible, create the matching expression index with an immutable expression. **Prevention.** Code review rule: no function or cast on a column in a WHERE clause on a large table; check the `Filter` line of every new query plan.

#### Incident 8: an implicit cast disables the index

**Scenario.** A support tool looks up orders by customer id using a `BigDecimal` parameter, bound through JDBC `setBigDecimal`. A migration changed the column type of the search field from `varchar` to `numeric` in the DTO, and the lookup became slow; the SQL text and the indexes did not change.

**Symptoms.** A lookup that took 0.2 ms takes 550 ms; the slow query appears in `pg_stat_statements` with `customer_id` `= $1` and a mean time of hundreds of milliseconds.

**Diagnosis.** Run the query with the same parameter type, for example `customer_id = 4242::numeric`: the plan is `Seq` `Scan` with `Filter: ((customer_id)::numeric = '4242'::numeric)`. The cast appears around the column. Comparing with `4242::bigint` returns the index plan at 0.19 ms.

**Root cause.** PostgreSQL has no `integer = numeric` operator inside the integer operator family; to compare, it converts the column of each row to numeric and then compares, which cannot use an index on the integer value. (MySQL behaves similarly when a string column is compared with a number: the column is converted for each row.)

**Fix.** Immediate: cast the parameter, not the column (`customer_id = CAST(? AS integer)`), or pass an `Integer` or `Long`. Permanent: keep parameter types aligned with column types in DTOs and repository method signatures (`findByCustomerId(Long id)`); in PostgreSQL JDBC avoid `setObject` with a type that does not match the column.

**Prevention.** Look for `::numeric`, `::text` or `CAST` around column names in the `Filter` line of plans; add a performance test that asserts an index scan for the key lookups.

#### Incident 9: deep OFFSET pagination gets slower on every page

**Scenario.** An admin screen pages through orders with `ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET :page * 20`. Early pages respond instantly; the export job that walks to the last page takes minutes and the database load rises as it proceeds.

**Symptoms.** Latency grows linearly with the page number; the plan of a deep page shows `actual rows=1000020` inside a `Limit` that returns 20.

**Diagnosis.**

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, created_at, amount FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000;

blocks.text:
`Index Scan ... actual rows=1000020` and `Buffers: shared hit=5 read=17719` (463 ms) against 4 buffers (0.05 ms) for the first page.

**Root cause.** The database cannot jump to the millionth row; it reads and discards everything before it. Concurrent inserts also make offset pages unstable, so rows may be skipped or repeated between requests.

**Fix.** Switch to keyset pagination: return the last `(created_at, id)` with each page and send it back as the cursor (`WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20`): 0.054 ms for any page. In Spring Data, `Window`/`ScrollPosition` with `KeysetScrollPosition` (Spring Data 3.1 and later) implements this; otherwise write the query with `@Query`.

**Prevention.** Use keyset pagination for any list that can grow beyond a few thousand rows, and for batch exports; reserve OFFSET for small, bounded result sets.

#### Incident 10: LIKE with a leading wildcard scans the whole table

**Scenario.** A product search runs `WHERE name LIKE '%M123456%'` on a table of one million products. A regular index on `name` exists, and the search is slow.

**Symptoms.** 220 ms per search and a plan with `Seq Scan` and `Filter: (name ~~ '%M123456%'::text)`.

**Diagnosis.** A B-tree orders by the beginning of the string; a pattern that starts with `%` has no usable prefix. Check the available extensions with `SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'pg_trgm'`.

**Root cause.** The condition is not an index condition for a B-tree. The sequential scan read 8384 pages (`shared` `hit=1153 read=7231`) and removed 999 999 rows.

**Fix.** Create a trigram GIN index:

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
 Bitmap Heap Scan on products  (cost=114.06..482.55 rows=100 width=34) (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (name ~~ '%M123456%'::text)
   Heap Blocks: exact=1
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_trgm  (actual rows=1 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared hit=22
 Execution Time: 0.728 ms

blocks.alt: pg_trgm: LIKE '%M123456%' becomes a lookup of trigrams, not a scan | pattern '%M123456%' m12 123 234 345 456 | m12 {18, 902, 40113, ...} | posting lists (sorted ctids) | 123 {18, 77, 5090, ...} | 456 {18, 6404, 99010, ...} | Measured, 1M rows: | Seq Scan 219 ms -> heap recheck | intersect lists -> candidate row 18 | GIN trigram 0.73 ms (exact LIKE) | Index 37 MB, heap 66 MB.

blocks.text:
The search dropped from 219 ms to 0.73 ms (300 times). The trigram index took 37 MB against a 66 MB table. Very short patterns (fewer than three characters) and very common fragments still yield many candidates; for ranked word search `tsvector` full-text search is the better tool, and for `ILIKE '%gaming mouse%'` the planner may still choose a sequential scan when it expects many matches (here it did, with a `Limit` that stopped after 10 rows). MySQL offers `FULLTEXT` indexes with `MATCH ... AGAINST` instead of trigrams.

**Prevention.** Decide early whether the feature is "search" (use full text or an external search engine) or "lookup" (use exact or prefix match), and do not use `LIKE '%x%'` on large tables for interactive features without a trigram index.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Explain the N+1 problem and how to fix it in Spring Data JPA. One query loads N parent entities and then one query per parent loads a lazy association, producing N+1 statements. Fix by fetching the association in the same statement (JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph), by batch fetching (default\_batch\_fetch\_size or @BatchSize, which turns N lookups into N/size IN queries), or by using a DTO projection that selects exactly the needed columns.

1. What does sargable mean? A predicate whose form lets the engine use an index to locate rows: the indexed column stands alone on one side of the comparison, with no function, arithmetic or cast applied.
2. Why does WHERE `YEAR(order_date) = 2024` hurt performance in MySQL? The function is evaluated for every row, so the index on `order_date` cannot be used; rewrite as a range `order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date <` `'2025-01-01'`.
3. Why is OFFSET pagination slow and what is the alternative? The server must generate and discard all skipped rows; keyset pagination filters by the last seen key and uses the index.
4. Is `COUNT(*)` faster than `COUNT(id)`? Not materially; both count rows (`COUNT(col)` skips NULLs). In PostgreSQL both scan the table or an index; for big tables use an estimate or a maintained counter.
5. How do you make `LIKE '%term%'` fast? A trigram GIN index (PostgreSQL), full-text search, or an external search engine; a B-tree cannot help.
6. When is `SELECT *` harmful? It reads every column, may include large TOAST values, prevents index-only scans, and breaks when columns are added; select the needed columns or use projections.
7. How do you rewrite a correlated subquery? Aggregate the inner table once in a derived table or CTE and join it, or use a window function or lateral join; the measured example went from 14.7 s to 64 ms.
8. How would you speed up `WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2`? Index both columns so the planner can use a bitmap OR, or rewrite as UNION ALL (disjoint) or UNION.
9. What is the cost of fetching a list with JPA entities when only two columns are displayed? Full entity hydration, extra associations and dirty-checking snapshots; a projection avoids all of it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Keep the indexed column bare in the predicate: ranges instead of functions, matching types instead of casts.
- Fewer rows and fewer columns: keyset pagination, projections, estimates instead of exact counts.
- Fewer round trips: fetch joins, entity graphs and batch fetching eliminate N+1.
- Rewrite correlated subqueries as a single aggregation and join; the work should happen once.
- Every claim should be checked with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after.

A production complaint rarely arrives as "the plan of statement 4711 has a wrong estimate". It arrives as "the checkout page is slow since Tuesday". Diagnosis therefore has two stages: **finding** which statement is responsible, and **explaining** why it is slow. The first stage uses aggregated statistics and logs; the second uses `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,` `BUFFERS)`, which earlier chapters of this part describe. This chapter sets up the instruments in PostgreSQL (`pg_stat_statements`, the slow-statement log, `auto_explain`, `pg_stat_activity`) and in MySQL (the slow query log, `performance_schema`, the `sys` schema), and ends with a repeatable procedure.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Three sources of evidence

blocks.caption: Three complementary instruments: the statement log records single slow executions, auto_explain adds the plan of those executions, and pg_stat_statements aggregates all executions by statement shape.
blocks.alt: application PostgreSQL backend | (Spring Boot, HikariCP) executes the statement | log_min_duration_statement auto_explain pg_stat_statements | statement text + duration plan with actual rows in the log calls, total/mean time, buffers | Log files answer 'which single execution was slow'; pg_stat_statements answers | 'which statement shape consumes the most time overall'.

blocks.text:
**Aggregated statistics** (`pg_stat_statements`) answer "which kind of statement consumes the most time in total". The extension normalises each statement (constants become `$1`, `$2`), and keeps cumulative counters: calls, total and mean time, rows, buffer hits and reads, temporary file use, WAL volume. It finds the death by a thousand cuts (a fast statement run millions of times, including the N+1 pattern) that no slow log would show.

**The slow-statement log** (`log_min_duration_statement`) answers "which individual execution was slow, and when". It records the statement text with its parameters and duration, so an incident can be tied to a time and a client.

`auto_explain` logs the *plan with actual row counts* of slow executions as they happen in production, which removes the guesswork of reproducing a problem that depends on parameter values, cache state or concurrent load.

#### pg_stat_statements

The module must be preloaded, which needs a server restart, and the extension created in each database:

blocks.code:
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
pg_stat_statements.track = all          # include statements nested in functions
compute_query_id = auto                 # on by default when the module is loaded
blocks.title: postgresql.conf

blocks.code:
CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements;
SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();      -- start a measurement window

blocks.text: After a workload, rank the statements. Total time identifies where the server spends its effort; mean time identifies slow individual statements; calls identify chatty code.

blocks.code:
SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 3)  AS mean_ms,
       rows,
       left(regexp_replace(query, '\s+', ' ', 'g'), 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE dbid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 6;

$ psql -d shop
 calls | total_ms | mean_ms | rows  | query
-------+----------+---------+-------+--------------------------------------------------------
  5000 |    309.7 |   0.062 | 75000 | select id, amount from orders where customer_id = $1
     1 |    186.8 | 186.815 |    15 | select * from orders where customer_id=$1::numeric
     1 |    184.6 | 184.601 |     1 | select count(*) from orders where date(created_at)=$1
     1 |    176.2 | 176.185 |     1 | select count(*) from orders where status=$1
   100 |      1.2 |   0.012 |  5000 | select id from customers where id <= $1
blocks.title: Output after a mixed workload (real)

blocks.text: Reading this output yields four findings without any plan: the first row is a statement called 5000 times, a repeated lookup (N+1 or a loop in application code); the second shows a cast in the query text; the third a function on a column; the fourth an aggregate that scans. Useful columns beyond these are `shared_blks_read` (disk-bound statements), `temp_blks_written` (spills), `rows / calls` (rows per call, which exposes unbounded results) and `stddev_exec_time` (unstable plans or parameter skew).

rows: Frequency and rows per call; high calls with few rows suggests N+1
Total cost to the server and typical latency (milliseconds)
Variability; a large spread suggests plan or parameter dependence
Pages from cache and from outside it; the stable measure of work
Log volume produced by write statements
Stable identifier to join with logs and other views
blocks.caption: Columns of pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL 16) used in diagnosis.

blocks.text:
#### The slow-statement log and auto_explain

`log_min_duration_statement` logs every statement that runs longer than the threshold; `0` logs all statements and `-1` disables it. A threshold of 100 to 500 ms is a common production starting point. `log_line_prefix` should include timestamp, process id, user, database and application name (`'%m [%p] %u@%d %a '`), so that entries can be correlated with application logs. Statements with parameter values are logged in full, which makes the log sensitive data; protect it accordingly.

blocks.code:
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '100ms';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();           -- no restart needed

$ psql -d shop
2026-10-18 06:57:40.931 ASIA [5046] LOG:  duration: 122.278 ms  statement: select count(*)
   from orders where status='CANCELLED'
blocks.title: Server log (real)

blocks.text: `auto_explain` is a loadable module. It can be loaded per session for a test (`LOAD 'auto_explain'`, superuser) or for all sessions with `session_preload_libraries` or `shared_preload_libraries`. With `log_analyze = on` it measures every statement, which has overhead, so use `auto_explain.sample_rate` or a high `log_min_duration` in production.

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop
2026-10-18 06:57:41.274 ASIA [5050] LOG:  duration: 283.924 ms  plan:
        Query Text: select count(*) from orders where status='PAID' and amount > 499;
        Aggregate  (cost=43335.40..43335.41 rows=1 width=8)
          (actual time=283.909..283.911 rows=1 loops=1)
          Buffers: shared hit=7845 read=12989
          ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..43334.00 rows=560 width=0)
                (actual time=0.079..283.686 rows=623 loops=1)
                Filter: ((amount > '499'::numeric) AND (status = 'PAID'::text))
                Rows Removed by Filter: 1499377
                Buffers: shared hit=7845 read=12989
blocks.title: Server log (real)

blocks.text:
The log entry is a complete diagnosis: a sequential scan that removes 1 499 377 rows to return 623, with estimate (560) close to actual (623). The estimate is right, so the fix is an index, not statistics.

#### What is running right now

`pg_stat_activity` lists sessions with their current statement, state and wait event. Long-running statements, sessions that are `idle in transaction`, and sessions waiting on locks are visible here.

blocks.code:
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       date_trunc('second', now() - query_start) AS running, left(query, 50) AS q
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'shop' AND state <> 'idle' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

$ psql -d shop
-[ RECORD 1 ]---+---------------------------------------------------
pid             | 9107
state           | active
wait_event_type | Timeout
wait_event      | PgSleep
running         | 00:00:01
q               | select count(*), pg_sleep(4) from orders where sta
blocks.title: Output (real; the statement includes pg_sleep(4) to stay running)

blocks.text:
A statement that is slow because it is **waiting** shows a `wait_event_type` of `Lock`, `IO` or `LWLock`; a statement that is slow because it is **working** shows `active` with no wait event. This distinction decides whether to look at the plan (working) or at locks, I/O and connections (waiting; see the part on transactions for locks). To stop a runaway statement use `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` (cancels the query) and, if needed, `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` (closes the connection).

#### MySQL instruments

rows: `slow_query_log = ON`, `long_query_time` (default 10 s; set to 0.1 to 1 s)
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` after the fact (8.0.18 and later); optimizer trace
blocks.caption: Slow-query tooling (MySQL 8.x documented; not run on the build machine).

blocks.text:
The ratio `sum_rows_examined / sum_rows_sent` is the MySQL counterpart of `Rows Removed by Filter`: a statement that examines 100 000 rows to send 10 is scanning. The slow log lines carry `Rows_examined` and `Rows_sent` for each execution in the same way.

blocks.text:
1. **Scope.** Which endpoint, since when, for which users or parameters? Compare with deployments, data growth and batch schedules.
2. **Locate.** Rank `pg_stat_statements` by `total_exec_time`, by `mean_exec_time` and by `calls`; check `pg_stat_activity` for current waits.
3. **Reproduce.** Run the statement with the real parameter values on production-like data, with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,` `BUFFERS)`. A statement that is fast on a developer database with a thousand rows proves nothing.
4. **Compare estimates with actuals** at every node; a tenfold difference means statistics or correlation (planner chapter).
5. **Find the dominant cost**: a scan that discards almost everything (`Rows Removed by Filter`), a loop count in the hundreds of thousands, a spill (`temp`), a join that multiplies rows, a sort of the entire result.
6. **Change one thing** (index, rewrite, statistics, setting) and run EXPLAIN again; compare buffers, then time.
7. **Verify in production** with `pg_stat_statements` after resetting the window, and keep the evidence (before and after plans) with the change.

### Worked example

#### From a complaint to a fix in five steps

**Complaint.** "The back-office order screens are slow in the afternoon."

Step 1: reset the window at the start of the afternoon peak and rank by total time after thirty minutes. The first row of the listing in this chapter is a statement called 5000 times with a mean of 0.062 ms, total 310 ms: its total is not the largest in the sample, but its call count is 50 times that of any other statement.

Step 2: the second and third rows are single executions at 185 ms. The query texts are `customer_id=$1::numeric` and `date(created_at)=$1`. Neither needs a plan to be suspected; each plan confirms it with a `Seq Scan` and a cast or function in the `Filter` line.

Step 3: fix each cause in the order of benefit.

rows: Accept the scan or restructure (partial index for a queue)

blocks.text:
*Findings, evidence and fixes in this order of impact (measured before and after on the 1.5 million row table).*

Step 4: the fourth row is not a defect. `status = $1` selects a fifth of the table, and a scan is the correct plan for that selectivity. Not every full scan is a problem; the diagnosis must separate scans that discard rows from scans that need most of them.

Step 5: reset `pg_stat_statements` after the deployment and confirm that the totals of the affected statements fell. The reset is part of the method, because cumulative counters carry the history.

### Hands-on

Enable the slow log, run a workload, then rank it.

blocks.code:
$ psql -d shop -c "SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset()"
$ pgbench -n -f nplus1.sql -t 100 -c 1 shop          # a workload script of your own
$ psql -d shop -c "SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric,1) total_ms, \
                   left(query,60) FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5"

blocks.text:
`pgbench` is the benchmarking tool shipped with PostgreSQL. A script file of SQL (with `\set` lines for random parameters) is replayed by `-c` clients for `-t` transactions or `-T` seconds, and it reports latency average and transactions per second. The N+1 and batched variants in this chapter were driven this way. On the build machine the 51-statement script averaged 7 to 11 ms per transaction and the equivalent 2-statement script 4 to 7 ms over a Unix-domain socket (measurements varied between runs because the machine is shared; the difference is dominated by statement count, and over a network with 0.5 ms round trip it grows by 0.5 ms per extra statement).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident 11: fast in psql, slow in the application

**Scenario.** A query runs in 2 ms in `psql` with literal values but takes 800 ms from the Spring Boot service for some customers. Developers cannot reproduce it.

**Symptoms.** Latency distribution is bimodal; `pg_stat_statements` shows a large `stddev_exec_time` and `max_exec_time` for the statement; the slow executions occur on pooled connections that have run the statement several times.

**Diagnosis.** Enable `auto_explain` for the application role with a threshold above the normal latency, and read the plan of a slow execution from the log:

The log shows the generic plan (parameters `$1`) with a nested loop for a customer who has 200 000 rows, estimated from the average. Compare with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` using the literal for the heavy customer.

**Root cause.** Server-side prepared statements switch to a generic plan after five executions, and the generic plan fits an average customer, not a very large one (data skew).

**Fix.** Immediate: `ALTER ROLE app SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan`. Permanent: keep the statistics current for the skewed column (`SET STATISTICS`), or route large customers through a different query.

**Prevention.** Test with the largest and the smallest tenant; keep `auto_explain` enabled with a conservative threshold so that such cases are caught the first time.

#### Incident 12: the slow query is found, but the table scan is the right plan

**Scenario.** A report on an audit table with 50 million rows scans the whole table daily. A developer adds an index on the filtered column to "fix" it; the planner ignores it, and the new index slows the writes of the audit table by 30 percent.

**Symptoms.** The new index has `idx_scan = 0`; the plan is unchanged; insert latency is higher.

**Diagnosis.** `EXPLAIN` shows `Seq Scan` with an estimate of 40 percent of rows returned, and the actual rows agree. The index cannot help a query that needs 40 percent of the table.

**Root cause.** The problem is the access pattern, not the plan: the report reads a large share of the data every day.

**Fix.** Drop the index (`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`). Reduce the work: precompute a daily summary table, use a materialised view refreshed after the load, partition the table by date so that each report reads one partition, or move the report to a replica. A covering index may help only if it makes the scan narrow enough for an index-only scan.

**Prevention.** Before adding an index, estimate selectivity from `pg_stats` and check that the predicate returns a small fraction; record the expected plan in the change request and confirm it afterwards.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: A query is slow in production. How do you investigate it? Locate the statement with pg\_stat\_statements or the slow log, reproduce it with the real parameters on realistic data, run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), compare estimated with actual rows, look for scans that discard rows, large loop counts, spills and sorts, change one thing at a time, and verify in production by comparing statistics before and after.

1. What does pg\_stat\_statements show that the slow query log does not? Aggregates by statement shape over all executions, so many fast executions (N+1) and total cost are visible; the log shows only single executions above a threshold.
2. How do you capture the plan of a query that is only slow sometimes? auto\_explain with a duration threshold, which logs the actual plan of slow executions including parameters-dependent plans.
3. How do you tell whether a slow statement is working or waiting? pg\_stat\_activity: an active session with no wait event is using CPU or I/O in its plan; a wait\_event\_type of Lock, IO or LWLock indicates waiting.
4. What are Rows\_examined and Rows\_sent in MySQL? The rows the engine read and the rows returned to the client; a large ratio indicates a scan or a weak index.
5. Why reset pg\_stat\_statements? The counters are cumulative since the last reset, so a measurement window around a change gives a clean before and after.
6. Why is average latency a poor metric? A few very slow executions hide behind a low mean; use the maximum, the standard deviation and percentiles from application metrics.
7. Is a sequential scan always a problem? No; it is correct for small tables and for predicates that return a large fraction of the rows.
8. What is the first thing to check in a plan? Estimated versus actual row counts at each node, then the node with the largest actual time or buffer count.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Find first, explain second: pg\_stat\_statements for totals and call counts, the slow log for single executions, auto\_explain for plans in production.
- Distinguish working from waiting with pg\_stat\_activity before reading any plan.
- A repeated cheap statement (high `calls`) is as costly to the application as a single slow statement is to the database.
- Change one thing at a time and compare buffers and time before and after; reset statistics to measure the effect in production.
- MySQL offers the same tools under different names: slow query log, performance\_schema digests and the sys schema.

A database that stores data but cannot protect it during change is of little use for an application that moves money, reserves seats, or decrements stock. A single business operation usually requires several SQL statements: a debit and a credit, an order row and its order lines, a stock decrement and a reservation. Between any two of these statements a process may crash, a constraint may fail, a network connection may drop, or another client may read or modify the same rows. A **transaction** is the mechanism that groups statements into one logical unit of work so that the database, and not the application, enforces correct behaviour in each of those situations.

This chapter defines the transaction abstraction, states the four ACID properties together with the specific failure each one prevents, and shows the behaviour on a real PostgreSQL 16 server. The remaining chapters of this Part examine how isolation, multiversion concurrency control, locking, write-ahead logging and the Java transaction API realise these guarantees.

### Concept and mechanism

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: A transaction is a sequence of database operations that the DBMS treats as a single unit with respect to failure and concurrency. It ends either with `COMMIT`, which makes all of its effects permanent and visible, or with `ROLLBACK`, which discards all of them.

#### The four ACID properties

**Atomicity** states that all operations of a transaction take effect, or none of them does. The failure prevented is a partially applied operation: a debit recorded without the matching credit. The DBMS implements atomicity by recording, for every row version a transaction creates, which transaction created it, and by consulting a durable record of each transaction outcome. A row version written by an aborted transaction is never returned to a reader. In PostgreSQL the abort path costs almost nothing because the old row versions remain in place; in InnoDB the old versions are restored from the undo log.

**Consistency** states that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state, where valid means that every declared integrity constraint holds: `PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `CHECK`, `NOT NULL`. The failure prevented is the visibility of data that violates a business rule. Consistency in the ACID sense is a joint responsibility. The DBMS enforces the declared constraints; the application is responsible for declaring all rules that matter. A rule that is not declared (for example "the sum of order line amounts equals the order total") is not protected by ACID. **Isolation** states that concurrently executing transactions do not observe each other's intermediate states. The failure prevented is a family of anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew) analysed in the next chapter. Isolation is configurable because the strongest form, serial execution, is also the most expensive.

**Durability** states that once the DBMS has acknowledged `COMMIT`, the effects survive a crash of the process, the operating system or the machine. The failure prevented is the loss of a confirmed commit. The mechanism is the write-ahead log: the log record describing the commit is forced to stable storage before the acknowledgement is sent.

blocks.text:
#### Transaction boundaries and states

A transaction begins explicitly with `BEGIN` (or `START TRANSACTION`) or implicitly with the first statement when the client library has disabled autocommit. It ends with `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. A transaction passes through the states shown below. The state "partially committed" exists between the moment the client issues `COMMIT` and the moment the commit record is durable; a failure to flush the log in that interval moves the transaction to the failed state.

blocks.text:
PostgreSQL has one notable behaviour. When a statement fails inside an explicit transaction block, the whole transaction enters an aborted state. Every following statement is rejected with `current transaction is aborted,` `commands ignored until end of transaction block` until `ROLLBACK` is issued. A `COMMIT` issued in this state is silently converted to a `ROLLBACK`, which the server reports through the command tag. MySQL InnoDB behaves differently: a failed statement rolls back only that statement, and the transaction stays usable, with the exceptions of deadlock and lock wait timeout in some configurations.

#### Autocommit

Under **autocommit**, every statement is its own transaction, committed as soon as it completes. PostgreSQL (psql and the JDBC driver by default) and MySQL both start in autocommit mode. Two consequences matter to application developers. First, a business operation consisting of two statements issued under autocommit is two transactions, and no atomicity exists between them. Second, JDBC disables autocommit when `Connection.setAutoCommit(false)` is called; Spring does this on behalf of the application when a `@Transactional` method starts.

rows: only the statement is rolled back
transactional; `CREATE TABLE` can be rolled back
implicit commit before and after most DDL
blocks.caption: Transaction control differences between PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.x (InnoDB).

blocks.text:
The fourth row has operational consequences. A schema migration that contains five DDL statements runs in a single atomic unit in PostgreSQL, so a failure at statement four leaves the schema unchanged. In MySQL the first three statements have already been committed, and the migration tool must be prepared for a half-migrated schema.

#### Savepoints

A **savepoint** marks a position inside a transaction to which the transaction can return without abandoning the work done before it. `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` undoes the statements issued after the savepoint and also clears the aborted state caused by an error in that region. Internally PostgreSQL implements a savepoint as a subtransaction with its own transaction identifier. JDBC exposes the feature through `Connection.setSavepoint()` and `rollback(Savepoint)`; Spring uses it for `Propagation.NESTED`.

### Worked example

The scenario is a transfer of 600 from alice to bob, where the table carries `CHECK (balance >= 0)` and alice holds 500. The expected result is that no balance changes, because the debit would violate the constraint.

blocks.text:
Trace of the steps:

1. `BEGIN` opens the transaction and assigns no transaction identifier yet; an identifier is allocated lazily at the first write.
2. `UPDATE ... balance = balance - 600 WHERE id = 1` creates a new row version with balance -100. The `CHECK` constraint is evaluated before the statement completes and rejects the row. The error aborts the transaction.
3. The credit to bob is refused without being executed, because the transaction is already aborted.
4. `COMMIT` has nothing to commit. The server answers `ROLLBACK`, and a later `SELECT` shows both balances unchanged.

### Hands-on

The following session ran on the build machine against PostgreSQL 16.15. The table is created and filled first.

blocks.title: setup.sql

blocks.text:
#### Rollback discards all changes

**psql session (real output)**

The asterisk in the prompt `t=*#` indicates an open transaction. Inside the transaction the session sees its own uncommitted changes; after `ROLLBACK` they are gone.

#### Constraint failure aborts the transaction

**psql session (real output)**

The prompt marker changes to `!` in the aborted state, and `COMMIT` returns the tag `ROLLBACK`. An application must therefore treat the exception of the failing statement as the end of the transaction and not rely on the outcome of a later `COMMIT`.

#### Savepoints isolate a failing statement

**psql session (real output)**

The duplicate insert failed, but the rollback to `s1` restored a usable transaction, and the rows for carol and dave were committed together. Rows 3 and 4 exist; the failing row never did.

#### Autocommit off in psql

**psql session (real output)**

With `AUTOCOMMIT off` psql opens a transaction implicitly before the first statement, which is what the JDBC call `setAutoCommit(false)` achieves for Java code.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: half a transfer after an application crash

**Scenario.** A legacy service executes the debit and the credit of a transfer as two separate JDBC calls on a connection in autocommit mode. The service host is restarted during a deployment.

**Symptoms.** A reconciliation job reports a total across all accounts that is lower than the total of the previous day by

1. One customer reports a debit with no corresponding credit.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Compare the sum of balances with the ledger of transfers.
2. Search the transfer log for transfers that have a debit entry without a credit entry.
3. Check the connection setting in the service: `SHOW AUTOCOMMIT` in MySQL, or in PostgreSQL the log with `log_statement = 'mod'`, which shows `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` around statements, or their absence.

blocks.code:
SELECT t.id, t.amount
FROM transfer_log t
LEFT JOIN ledger_entry c ON c.transfer_id = t.id AND c.side = 'CREDIT'
WHERE c.id IS NULL;
blocks.title: reconcile.sql

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The two statements were separate transactions. The first committed immediately; the process terminated before the second one was sent, so atomicity was never available.

**Fix.** Immediate: for every orphaned debit, apply the missing credit inside a transaction that also marks the transfer as repaired. Permanent: execute both statements within one transaction, with `@Transactional` on the service method or the explicit `setAutoCommit(false)` pattern above.

**Prevention.** Enable an integration test that terminates the connection between the two statements (for example through `pg_terminate_backend`) and asserts that the balances are unchanged. Declare double-entry invariants through a deferred constraint trigger or by periodic reconciliation.

#### Incident: migration half applied on MySQL

**Scenario.** A release script adds a column, back-fills it and adds a `NOT NULL` constraint. The back-fill statement fails with a data error.

**Symptoms.** The application fails at startup because the schema is in an intermediate state: the column exists but is nullable. Re-running the migration fails with `Duplicate column name`.

**Diagnosis.** `SHOW CREATE TABLE` reveals the intermediate schema. The migration tool history table (for example `flyway_schema_history`) marks the migration as failed.

**Root cause.** MySQL commits implicitly before and after each DDL statement, so the first `ALTER TABLE` could not be rolled back together with the failing statement. In PostgreSQL the same migration, run inside a single transaction, would leave no trace.

**Fix.** Immediate: manually drop the column or complete the migration, then repair the migration history. Permanent: split the migration into idempotent steps (`ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` is available in MariaDB and PostgreSQL but not in MySQL 8.0, which requires a guard through `information_schema`).

**Prevention.** Keep each migration to one DDL statement on MySQL; on PostgreSQL rely on transactional DDL, with the exceptions of statements such as `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which cannot run inside a transaction block.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What does ACID stand for, and which property does a write-ahead log mainly provide? Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. The write-ahead log provides durability, because the commit record is flushed before the acknowledgement, and it also supports atomicity, because recovery can identify and ignore the effects of transactions without a commit record.

1. Which ACID property is the responsibility of the application rather than the DBMS? Consistency. The DBMS enforces declared constraints only; business rules that are not declared as constraints are not protected.
2. What happens in PostgreSQL after an error inside a transaction block? The transaction is marked aborted, and every statement fails until `ROLLBACK` or `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`. `COMMIT` performs a rollback.
3. Does DDL participate in transactions? In PostgreSQL, yes, with a few exceptions such as `CREATE INDEX` `CONCURRENTLY`. In MySQL, DDL causes an implicit commit.
4. What is autocommit and why does it matter for atomicity? Every statement is its own transaction. Two statements executed in autocommit mode are not atomic as a pair.
5. What is a savepoint used for? It allows the rollback of part of a transaction, for example to continue after a failing insert. Spring `NESTED` propagation maps to it.
6. Can a committed transaction be lost? Only if durability is relaxed (`synchronous_commit = off`, `fsync = off`, a volatile disk cache) or storage is damaged. The next chapters quantify this.
7. Does a read-only query need a transaction? Every statement runs in a transaction. Explicit read-only transactions (`BEGIN READ ONLY`) additionally provide a stable snapshot at higher isolation levels.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A transaction groups statements into an all-or-nothing unit; `COMMIT` publishes, `ROLLBACK` discards.
- Atomicity and durability depend on the log; isolation depends on MVCC and locks; consistency depends on declared constraints.
- PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction on a statement error; savepoints contain the damage. MySQL rolls back only the failing statement.
- PostgreSQL DDL is transactional; MySQL DDL commits implicitly.
- Autocommit makes every statement its own transaction, so multi-statement business operations need an explicit transaction.

Isolation answers the question of what one transaction may observe while others execute at the same time. The ideal, called **serializability**, states that the outcome of any concurrent execution equals the outcome of some serial execution of the same transactions. Enforcing it for every workload is expensive, so the SQL standard defines weaker **isolation levels** that tolerate named anomalies in exchange for higher throughput. The choice of level is a correctness decision, and the defaults differ between engines: PostgreSQL defaults to `READ COMMITTED`, MySQL InnoDB to `REPEATABLE READ`.

This chapter defines each anomaly, reproduces it with two real sessions on PostgreSQL 16.15, and then states what each level in PostgreSQL and in MySQL InnoDB permits. All outputs labelled real were produced on the build machine with two `psql` sessions, A and B, executing the listed statements in the order given.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Anomalies

- **Dirty read.** Transaction A reads a change made by transaction B that has not committed. If B rolls back, A has used data that never existed.
- **Non-repeatable read.** A reads a row twice and obtains different values because B committed an update between the two reads.
- **Phantom read.** A executes the same predicate query twice and obtains different sets of rows because B committed an insert or delete that matches the predicate.
- **Lost update.** A and B both read a value, compute a new value in the application, and write it back; the second write overwrites the first, which is lost.
- **Write skew.** A and B each read an overlapping set of rows, then write to different rows in a way that together violates an invariant that each transaction preserved on its own.

#### The standard levels and what the engines implement

The SQL standard defines the four levels `READ UNCOMMITTED`, `READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ` and `SERIALIZABLE` through the anomalies each one forbids. The definitions are loose, and real engines implement the levels with snapshots or locks in ways that do not match the standard table exactly. The matrix below describes the actual behaviour of the two engines.

blocks.text:
#### Snapshot isolation versus locking

PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ are built on MVCC snapshots, described in the next chapter: a reader never blocks a writer and a writer never blocks a reader. The difference between the two levels is the lifetime of the snapshot. In READ COMMITTED every statement obtains a new snapshot, so two statements of one transaction can disagree. In REPEATABLE READ one snapshot is taken at the first statement and kept until the end, so all statements agree.

A write-write conflict is handled by waiting for the other transaction. When the other transaction commits, behaviour depends on the level. In READ COMMITTED the waiting statement re-reads the newest committed version of the row and re-evaluates its `WHERE` clause (the **EvalPlanQual** step), and then proceeds. In REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE the waiting statement cannot proceed against a row that changed after its snapshot, so it fails with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (SQLSTATE 40001). The application must retry the whole transaction.

**SSI** extends snapshot isolation with detection of dangerous read-write dependency patterns, as shown below. Transactions record what they read using predicate-like **SIREAD locks**, which never block. When two concurrent transactions each read data the other writes (two consecutive read-write antidependencies in a cycle), one of them is aborted with SQLSTATE 40001.

blocks.text:
InnoDB uses an alternative design. A plain `SELECT` under REPEATABLE READ reads from a read view (a snapshot built from undo logs). Locking reads (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) and writes always operate on the latest committed row, not the snapshot, and use **next-key locks**, a combination of a record lock and a gap lock on the index range scanned, which prevents other transactions from inserting into that range and thereby prevents phantoms for locking statements. Because `UPDATE` reads the latest version, an increment such as `SET balance = balance - 50` does not lose updates under any InnoDB level; a read-modify-write cycle with the value computed in the application can lose updates under REPEATABLE READ, because the plain `SELECT` reads the snapshot.

### Worked example

The following step-by-step trace uses the lost update scenario. The account balance is 500. Session A withdraws 100 and session B withdraws 50. The application reads the balance, subtracts the amount, and writes the result.

blocks.text:
1. A and B start at READ COMMITTED. Both `SELECT balance` and receive 500.00.
2. A writes `balance = 500 - 100` and commits. The row holds 400.
3. B writes `balance = 500 - 50` (the 500 is a Java variable) and commits. The row holds 450. The first write is lost.

Replacing the write by `UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1` changes step 3: B waits for A to commit, re-reads the row (400), and computes 350. The result is correct without any change of isolation level.

### Hands-on

The table used throughout is `account(id, owner, balance)` with rows (1, alice, 500.00) and (2, bob, 100.00). Each experiment starts from this state.

#### Dirty read is impossible in PostgreSQL

**two sessions, real output**

B requested `READ UNCOMMITTED` and still saw the committed value 500.00. PostgreSQL treats the level as `READ` `COMMITTED`.

#### Non-repeatable read at READ COMMITTED

**two sessions, real output**
The same query inside one transaction returned 500.00 and then 450.00. See the sequence diagram that follows for the interleaving.

blocks.text:
#### Phantom read at READ COMMITTED, none at REPEATABLE READ

**two sessions, real output**

At READ COMMITTED the aggregate changed from 2 rows to 3 within one transaction. At REPEATABLE READ the inserted row 4 stayed invisible, so PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ also prevents phantoms, which is stronger than the standard demands.

#### Lost update by read-modify-write

**two sessions, real output**

The correct final balance is 350.00. The debit of 100 vanished without any error.

#### The atomic update avoids the anomaly

**two sessions, real output**

B blocked until A committed, then re-evaluated against the committed row 400.00 and wrote 350.00.

#### REPEATABLE READ detects the conflict instead

**two sessions, real output**

The error is a signal to retry the transaction from the beginning; the lost update is converted into a visible failure.

#### Write skew with doctors on call

The business rule is that at least one doctor must stay on call. The table is `doctor(name, on_call)` with alice and bob both on call.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: lost update on a balance

**Scenario.** A Spring Data JPA service loads an `Account` entity, calls `account.setBalance(account.getBalance().subtract(amount))` and lets the persistence context flush at commit. Two requests for the same account overlap.

**Symptoms.** The ledger shows two withdrawals but the balance has been reduced by only one. No exception is logged.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Identify the pattern in the SQL log (`spring.jpa.show-sql=true` or `log_statement = 'mod'`): two `SELECT` statements followed by two `UPDATE account SET balance=? WHERE id=?` with literal values rather than an expression.
2. Compare the sum of ledger entries with the stored balance for the affected account.

blocks.code:
SELECT a.id, a.balance, COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0) AS ledger_sum
FROM account a LEFT JOIN ledger l ON l.account_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.balance
HAVING a.balance <> 1000 + COALESCE(SUM(l.amount), 0);
blocks.title: diagnose_lost_update.sql

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The read-modify-write cycle computed the new balance from a stale value at READ COMMITTED, as in the worked example.

**Fix.** Immediate: repair affected balances from the ledger. Permanent, in order of preference: (1) an atomic statement `UPDATE account SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amount`, checking the update count; (2) optimistic locking with `@Version`, where the update carries `WHERE version = ?` and a zero update count raises `OptimisticLockingFailureException`; (3) `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (`@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)`) before the read.

#### Incident: overselling and double booking

**Scenario.** A shop sells the last unit of an item. Two checkout requests check `stock > 0`, both see 1, and both proceed. The same pattern applies to seat reservations where the check and the insert are separate statements.

**Symptoms.** Two orders exist for one unit; stock is zero or, without a constraint, negative.

**Diagnosis.** Compare ordered quantities with stock, and look for two committed transactions whose reads preceded each other's writes.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The condition was evaluated in a read that was separate from the write, so the check-then-act sequence was not atomic. For seats, a missing `UNIQUE (event_id, seat_no)` constraint removes the last defence.

**Fix.** Use the guarded `UPDATE` and treat `UPDATE 0` as "sold out". Back it with `CHECK (stock >= 0)`. For seats and other inserts, declare `UNIQUE (event_id, seat_no)` and handle the unique violation (SQLSTATE 23505).

**Prevention.** Encode every invariant as a constraint, and write the application code so that the write statement carries the condition.

#### Incident: write skew on on-call doctors

**Scenario.** Two doctors request leave at the same time. The service counts doctors on call and permits the request if more than one remains.

**Symptoms.** A morning audit finds zero doctors on call. Neither transaction raised an error.

**Diagnosis.** The two update transactions overlap in time and touch different rows, which is the signature of write skew. Confirm with `SHOW transaction_isolation;` and the application log of both requests.

**Root cause.** At REPEATABLE READ (and READ COMMITTED) the decision is based on a snapshot that the other transaction invalidates by writing a different row.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore the on-call roster manually. Permanent, one of: run the transaction at `SERIALIZABLE` and retry on SQLSTATE 40001; lock the rows read with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`; or materialise the conflict by locking a single parent row (for example the ward) that every leave request must update.

### Questions to expect

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL and in MySQL InnoDB, and what follows from the difference? PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED and InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ. Code that is correct under one default can break under the other: a read-modify-write that raises no error in READ COMMITTED may raise a serialization failure in PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, while InnoDB REPEATABLE READ silently permits it for plain selects.

1. Define a phantom read. A repeated predicate query returns a different set of rows because another transaction committed a matching insert or delete. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ prevents it through the snapshot; InnoDB prevents it for locking reads through next-key locks.
2. How is a lost update prevented? By an atomic `UPDATE ... SET x = x - ?`, by `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, by a version column checked in the `WHERE` clause, or by REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL with retry.
3. What is write skew and which level prevents it in PostgreSQL? Two transactions read overlapping data and update disjoint rows, violating an invariant. Only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) prevents it automatically; RR and RC do not.
4. What does SQLSTATE 40001 mean and what must the application do? A serialization failure or deadlock. Retry the entire transaction, not only the failed statement.
5. Does `READ UNCOMMITTED` in PostgreSQL permit dirty reads? No. It behaves as READ COMMITTED.
6. How does PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE differ from MySQL SERIALIZABLE? PostgreSQL uses non-blocking SSI with aborts; InnoDB turns plain reads into shared locking reads and blocks, with more deadlocks.
7. Why does a higher level not always mean a safer application? The application must handle aborts and retries; without retries a higher level converts silent anomalies into visible errors, which is an improvement but still a defect.
8. When is READ COMMITTED sufficient? When each business operation is expressed through atomic statements or explicit row locks, and no multi-statement decision depends on a consistent view.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- An anomaly is defined by what a transaction can observe; each isolation level forbids a subset of anomalies.
- PostgreSQL: RC takes a snapshot per statement, RR per transaction, SERIALIZABLE adds SSI conflict detection; no dirty reads at any level.
- InnoDB: default REPEATABLE READ with a read view for plain reads and next-key locks for locking reads.
- Lost updates are fixed by atomic updates, row locks or version columns; write skew needs SERIALIZABLE with retry or explicit locking.
- Serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) require a retry of the whole transaction.

Lock-based concurrency control makes readers wait for writers and writers wait for readers. **Multiversion** **concurrency control (MVCC)** removes most of this waiting by keeping several versions of a row at the same time: a writer creates a new version and leaves the old version in place, and every reader selects the version that was current at the moment of its snapshot. The price is that obsolete versions accumulate and must be removed by a background process, which in PostgreSQL is called **VACUUM**. Most operational problems of PostgreSQL, from table bloat to transaction identifier wraparound, are consequences of this design, so a working model of it is required for diagnosis.

This chapter examines the PostgreSQL implementation with real output from `pageinspect`, then summarises the InnoDB approach for comparison.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Row versions and system columns

Every table in PostgreSQL is a heap of 8 kB pages. Each row version, a **tuple**, starts with a 23-byte header whose first fields are the identifier of the transaction that created it (`xmin`), the identifier of the transaction that deleted or locked it (`xmax`, zero while the tuple is live) and the tuple's own location or the location of its successor (`ctid`, a pair of block number and line pointer offset). These fields are visible to SQL as system columns.

blocks.text:
An `UPDATE` never modifies a tuple in place. It marks the old tuple with its own transaction identifier in `xmax` and writes a new tuple with the same identifier in `xmin`; the old tuple's `t_ctid` points to the new one. A `DELETE` only sets `xmax`. Rolled-back changes leave tuples whose creating transaction aborted; they are invisible to every snapshot.

#### Snapshots

A **snapshot** is a compact description of which transactions count as committed at a point in time. It consists of `xmin` (the lowest transaction identifier still in progress), `xmax` (the first identifier not yet assigned) and the list `xip` of identifiers in progress between them. `pg_current_snapshot()` prints it as `xmin:xmax:xip_list`. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE take one at the first statement.

blocks.text:
#### Visibility rules

A tuple is visible to a snapshot when its inserter is visible and no visible transaction has deleted it. The decision sequence is shown in the figure. In practice PostgreSQL consults the commit log (`pg_xact`) to learn whether a transaction committed, and caches the answer in **hint bits** in the tuple's `t_infomask` so that later readers skip the lookup. A tuple whose xmax is only a row lock (as set by `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) remains visible.

blocks.text:
#### HOT updates and line pointers

Each page begins with an array of line pointers (`lp`) that point to tuples inside the page. Indexes store the page number and line pointer offset. When an update does not change any indexed column and the new version fits in the same page, PostgreSQL creates a **heap-only tuple (HOT)**: the old tuple points to the new one through `t_ctid`, and no index entry is added. Pruning later turns the first line pointer into a redirect, so index entries remain valid. This is why updates of non-indexed columns are much cheaper than updates of indexed ones.

#### VACUUM and autovacuum

VACUUM scans a table, finds tuples that are dead to every current and future snapshot, removes them (and their index entries), and records the freed space in the free space map so later inserts can reuse it. Plain VACUUM does not return space to the operating system, except for empty pages at the end of the file. `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table into a new file, which reclaims space but holds an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration.

**Autovacuum** launches VACUUM and ANALYZE automatically. A table is vacuumed when the number of dead tuples exceeds `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * reltuples`. The defaults observed on the build cluster are 50 and 0.2, so a table of 10 million rows is vacuumed only after about 2 million dead tuples. Large hot tables therefore commonly receive per-table settings.

#### The removable horizon

VACUUM may remove a dead tuple only when no snapshot can still need it. The oldest transaction identifier that any session might still need is the **horizon**. A session that holds an open transaction holds back the horizon: its transaction identifier, or its snapshot if it has read data, defines the oldest tuple version that must be kept. A transaction that is idle but open therefore blocks cleanup for the entire database cluster, not just for the tables it touched.

blocks.text:
#### Transaction identifier wraparound

Transaction identifiers are 32-bit counters that wrap around. PostgreSQL compares two identifiers modulo 2^32: an identifier is in the past when it is less than 2^31 behind the current one. A tuple that stays unvacuumed for 2^31 transactions would appear to come from the future and vanish from every query. To prevent this, VACUUM **freezes** old tuples, replacing the inserter's identifier with a special state that is visible to all snapshots. `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` (default 200 000 000) forces an anti-wraparound autovacuum on tables whose `relfrozenxid` age exceeds it, even if autovacuum is otherwise disabled. If the age reaches within 40 million of the limit, the server warns; within three million of the limit, it stops accepting commands that assign new transaction identifiers.

blocks.text:
#### InnoDB for comparison

InnoDB stores the newest version of a row in the clustered index and keeps previous versions in **undo logs**. Each row carries a transaction identifier (`DB_TRX_ID`) and a roll pointer (`DB_ROLL_PTR`) to the undo record that can reconstruct the preceding version. A consistent read builds a **read view** (list of active transaction identifiers) and walks the undo chain until it reaches a version visible to that view. A background **purge** thread removes undo records that no read view requires. A long-running transaction therefore causes growth of the undo tablespace and of the history list length, the InnoDB counterpart of PostgreSQL bloat.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

The following steps use the real data of the next section. A table `acct(id, bal)` holds (1, 100) and (2, 200), inserted by transaction 778. Autovacuum is disabled for the table so that the versions stay visible.

1. Transaction 780 runs `UPDATE acct SET bal = 150 WHERE id = 1`. Tuple lp 1 gets `xmax = 780`; a new tuple lp 3 is written with `xmin = 780`, and lp 1 points to it through `t_ctid = (0,3)`.
2. Session A opens a transaction, `txid_current()` returns 781, and it runs `UPDATE acct SET bal = 175 WHERE id =` `1` without committing. Tuple lp 3 gets `xmax = 781`, and lp 4 is created with `xmin = 781`.
3. Session B takes a snapshot, `pg_current_snapshot()` returning `781:783:781`: the lowest active identifier is 781, the next unassigned is 783, and 781 is in progress.
4. Visibility check by session B for each tuple of row 1:

- – lp 1: `xmin 778` is committed and below 781. `xmax 780` is committed and below 781, so the deletion is visible. The tuple is invisible.
- – lp 3: `xmin 780` is visible. `xmax 781` is in the in-progress list, so that deletion is not visible to this snapshot. The tuple is visible, with `bal = 150`.
- – lp 4: `xmin 781` is in progress, so the insertion is not visible. The tuple is invisible.

1. Session B therefore reads `bal = 150` with `xmax = 781`, exactly as the real output below shows. Once transaction 781 commits, a new snapshot sees lp 4 and not lp 3.

### Hands-on

The cluster was PostgreSQL 16.15 with the `pageinspect` extension. Transaction identifiers are typical values of this run.

#### System columns after an update

**psql session (real output)**

blocks.code:
t=# SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM acct ORDER BY id;
 xmin | xmax | ctid  | id | bal
------+------+-------+----+-----
  778 |    0 | (0,1) |  1 | 100
  778 |    0 | (0,2) |  2 | 200

t=# UPDATE acct SET bal = 150 WHERE id = 1;
t=# SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM acct ORDER BY id;
 xmin | xmax | ctid  | id | bal
------+------+-------+----+-----
  780 |    0 | (0,3) |  1 | 150
  778 |    0 | (0,2) |  2 | 200

blocks.text:
The updated row moved from `ctid (0,1)` to `(0,3)`, and its `xmin` changed from 778 to 780. The row with id 2 is untouched.

#### Reading the page with pageinspect

blocks.code:
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid,
       (t_infomask & 256) > 0   AS xmin_commit,
       (t_infomask & 2048) > 0  AS xmax_invalid,
       (t_infomask2 & 16384) > 0 AS hot_updated,
       t_data
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct', 0));
blocks.title: heap_page_items.sql

blocks.text: **result (real output)**

Tuple 1 is the old version: `t_xmax = 780`, `t_ctid` pointing to tuple 3, and the HOT flag. `t_data` shows the integers in little-endian form: `0x64` is 100, `0x96` is 150.

#### An uncommitted update seen from another session

**two sessions, real output**

blocks.code:
A: BEGIN; SELECT txid_current();      -- 781
A: UPDATE acct SET bal = 175 WHERE id = 1;
B: SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM acct WHERE id = 1;
 xmin | xmax | ctid  | id | bal
------+------+-------+----+-----
  780 |  781 | (0,3) |  1 | 150

B: SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct',0)) ORDER BY lp;
 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------
  1 |    778 |    780 | (0,3)
  2 |    778 |      0 | (0,2)
  3 |    780 |    781 | (0,4)
  4 |    781 |      0 | (0,4)

B: SELECT pg_current_snapshot();
 781:783:781

blocks.text:
The page contains both versions, and session B reads the old one. The `xmax` of 781 in the result of B's query is the pending update, not yet effective.

#### DELETE, VACUUM and line pointers

**psql session (real output)**

blocks.code:
t=# DELETE FROM acct WHERE id = 2;
t=# SELECT lp, lp_flags, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct',0));

----+----------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |        1 |    778 |    780 | (0,3)
  2 |        1 |    778 |    783 | (0,2)
  3 |        1 |    780 |    781 | (0,4)
  4 |        1 |    781 |      0 | (0,4)

t=# VACUUM acct;
t=# SELECT lp, lp_flags, lp_off, t_xmin, t_xmax FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct',0));
 lp | lp_flags | lp_off | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+----------+--------+--------+--------

  2 |        0 |      0 |        |
  3 |        0 |      0 |        |
  4 |        1 |   8160 | 781    | 0

blocks.text:
#### Row locks live in xmax too

**psql session (real output)**

blocks.code:
t=# BEGIN; SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
t=*# SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax,
       (t_infomask & 128) > 0 AS lock_only, (t_infomask & 64) > 0 AS excl_lock
     FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct',0)) WHERE lp = 4;
 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | lock_only | excl_lock
----+--------+--------+-----------+-----------
  4 |    781 |    784 | t         | t

blocks.text:
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` writes the locking transaction identifier into `xmax` and sets the lock-only and exclusive-lock bits; no new tuple version is created. This is the reason a long `FOR UPDATE` workload still causes page writes.

#### Bloat reproduced: an open transaction versus VACUUM

The table `orders_b` had 100 000 rows and autovacuum disabled. Session B opened a transaction and requested its identifier (`txid_current()`) without further activity; session A then updated every row twice.

**psql session (real output)**

blocks.code:
t=# SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_b')) AS heap,
          pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_b_pkey')) AS pk;
  heap   |   pk
---------+---------
 4328 kB | 2208 kB

t=# SELECT pid, state, backend_xid, now() - xact_start AS xact_age FROM pg_stat_activity
    WHERE datname = 't' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();
 pid  |        state        | backend_xid |    xact_age
------+---------------------+-------------+-----------------
 3342 | idle in transaction |         788 | 00:00:00.601725

t=# UPDATE orders_b SET status = 'PAID';  UPDATE orders_b SET status = 'SHIPPED';
UPDATE 100000
UPDATE 100000
t=# SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_b')) AS heap, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup
    FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'orders_b';
 heap  | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup
-------+------------+------------
 13 MB |     200000 |     100000

blocks.text: The heap tripled although the logical data did not grow. The counter `n_dead_tup` is an estimate maintained by the statistics system. **VACUUM while session B is still open (real output, excerpt)**

blocks.code:
t=# VACUUM VERBOSE orders_b;
INFO:  finished vacuuming "t.public.orders_b": index scans: 0
pages: 0 removed, 1622 remain, 1622 scanned (100.00% of total)
tuples: 0 removed, 300000 remain, 200000 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 788, which was 14 XIDs old when operation ended

blocks.text:
`200000 are dead but not yet removable` and `removable cutoff: 788` identify the cause: the horizon is 788, the identifier of session B, so no tuple deleted after that identifier can be removed.

**VACUUM after session B committed (real output, excerpt)**

blocks.code:
t=# VACUUM VERBOSE orders_b;
INFO:  finished vacuuming "t.public.orders_b": index scans: 1
pages: 0 removed, 1622 remain, 1622 scanned (100.00% of total)
tuples: 200000 removed, 100000 remain, 0 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 802, which was 0 XIDs old when operation ended
index scan needed: 1082 pages from table (66.71% of total) had 200000 dead item identifiers removed
index "orders_b_pkey": pages: 825 in total, 0 newly deleted, 0 currently deleted, 0 reusable
WAL usage: 4608 records, 1 full page images, 1566512 bytes

t=# SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders_b')) AS heap, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup
    FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'orders_b';
 heap  | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup
-------+------------+------------
 13 MB |     100000 |          0

blocks.text:
All 200 000 dead tuples were removed, but the file kept its size of 13 MB. The freed space is reusable by later updates; it was not returned to the operating system. A further full-table update followed by plain VACUUM leaves the size at 13 MB (real result), whereas `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table:

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: idle in transaction blocks VACUUM and bloats tables

**Scenario.** A Spring service opens a transaction through `@Transactional`, calls a slow remote payment API inside the method, and in some failure paths never finishes because of a missing client timeout. Alternatively a developer leaves `BEGIN` open in a SQL console.

**Symptoms.** Table sizes grow week after week without data growth; queries on hot tables slow down; autovacuum runs repeatedly yet `n_dead_tup` remains high; disk usage alarms fire.

**Diagnosis.** Follow the decision path below.
